effect_mechanism: Restoring the hydrology and the vegetation of a drained or degraded wetland puts back the conditions a wetland biota needs — standing water, saturated soil, a vegetated surface — and species return from whatever source is in reach. Pooled across global meta-analysis, restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity by 19% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1], significantly for vertebrates (+53%), vascular plants (+45%) and terrestrial (+17%) and aquatic (+15%) invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3]. Creating wetlands in a farmed catchment works the same way from a lower base, by adding aquatic habitat to a landscape that has lost it: catchment-scale creation benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats was increased by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1], each additional created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species to regional richness with a median of 2.70, and the accumulation curve had not flattened after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so the regional species pool and its metapopulations keep gaining as more are built [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. What is done on the site matters as much as the water: a planted basin remained more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than an identical unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7], planting salt marsh improved biodiversity conservation against degraded wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5], and active restoration or replacement measures are needed to speed up vegetation recolonisation on bare peat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10]. In the tropics, rewetting a retired pulpwood plantation left 57 native peat-swamp-forest tree species growing spontaneously, in high densities, in the most rewetted conditions [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], and restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is expected to enhance biodiversity alongside its other benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4]. On the coast, reinstating tidal flow produced biodiversity gains in 57% of monitoring studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1], and of the studies with species-specific data 77% reported positive effects on at least one commercially important fish species and 34% on invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3]. Project reporting adds a European floodplain case: after the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes on the Danube, park reports cited in the World Bank completion report record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50, with mallard rising from 16 to 400 and rare birds such as purple heron and glossy ibis returning [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1]; in Moldova a project-supported inventory found that flora and fauna began to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland was restored [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2]; and in Belarus, vegetation mapping after rewetting 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland found Phragmites-sedge communities on at least 398 ha, against no more than 20 ha at baseline [ev_wgy_blr_7]. A review of floodplain wetland restoration studies finds the same direction in how projects report themselves: most published studies deemed their restoration activities successful or partially successful, irrespective of the restoration activity performed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1].
conditionality: The baseline is the degraded wetland, and that is what the gains are measured against. Where restored sites were compared with intact references they came close without matching: biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1], and the Swedish created wetlands were only almost as beneficial to biodiversity as mature reference ponds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. A shortfall against an intact reference is incomplete recovery, not harm done by the practice. The measured harm in this row comes from the peatland and tidal syntheses, and it is about how the restoration is done. Walking away from a degraded peatland is modelled as stagnating and even further deteriorating conditions more than 50 years after abandonment [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6], with Sphagnum recovery under passive restoration projected over centuries rather than decades [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5]. For specialist plant diversity the same synthesis gives no clear answer either way: enhanced restoration with active revegetation reached intact levels of that diversity within about 8 years, but the response to removing the stressor alone was slightly negative on average and the authors state they could not reliably predict the response, so this finding is carried as no strong evidence either way and is not counted as harm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8]. On the coast, negative outcomes from tidal reinstatement were rare at 12% of studies reviewed, but a notable documented case had a non-native predator of the critically endangered native fish as the most abundant species at the restoration site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. Not every component responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4], and macrobenthos abundance and biomass showed no major difference after salt-marsh planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. Reading cautions. The tidal review counts an outcome as positive when it improves on the tidally restricted condition even if it does not reach a pristine reference, which its authors say may overestimate positive outcomes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1]; and the Sumatran regrowth is a bundled intervention — canal blocking together with clearing part of the plantation, on plots close to remaining forest that supplies the seed — so none of it is attributable to rewetting alone [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3]. Project evaluations need the same care. The Bulgarian figures are park reports relayed by the completion report and taken within months of the first flooding, so they show a fast early response, not a settled community [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2]. The Belarus gain fell short of its own target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent in the donor bogs for three years, and reed and cattail colonised first on most of the prepared area [ev_wgy_blr_7]. The only lower-middle-income unit is thin and bundled: in Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage collectors are said to offer adequate living conditions for fauna and flora on anecdotal evidence from site visits and committee reports, inside a bundled drainage and irrigation programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]; no unit comes from a low-income country. The floodplain review is a vote count of authors' own declared success against indicators they chose, not a measured effect against a baseline, and its authors warn that unsuccessful outcomes are likely under-reported [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1]; it also relays a before-and-after study in which hydrological restoration of inundation levels failed to restore invertebrate food sources for birds, likely because of vague aims and predictions of what the target species required [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_2]. Most of the evidence sits in high- and upper-middle-income countries across Europe, North America, Australia, China and Southeast Asia, so transfer to a low-income rural setting is an assumption, not a finding.

effect_mechanism: On tropical peat, rewetting removes the drainage stress that keeps the site degraded, and where seed can still arrive the native community returns without planting: native peat-swamp-forest tree species were found growing spontaneously, at high density, in the most rewetted conditions of a restoration area (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to deliver enhanced biodiversity alongside litter supply to the upper peat, a stabilised microclimate and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
conditionality: Neither unit isolates the practice, so this row carries direction and nothing about size or speed. The Sumatran observation is explicitly a best case: every plot lay close to remaining forest, so seed arrival is easy, and the regrowth cannot be separated from the earlier clearing or from that seed proximity - no share of the outcome is attributed to rewetting alone (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). The companion statement is a potential the authors expect, not a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). Both come from upper-middle-income Southeast Asian peatlands, neither reports a comparison with an intact reference nor a time to recovery, and neither is from a low-income or farmed landscape - so for a humid-tropics scan this is a plausible-direction flag that needs local monitoring evidence before any magnitude is claimed, with distance to remaining forest the first thing to check on the ground.

effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income tropical peatland, the operative step is rewetting: removing the drainage stress lets the native community re-establish where a seed source remains, with native peat-swamp-forest tree species growing spontaneously and at high density in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to enhance biodiversity alongside litter supply, microclimate stabilisation and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). conditionality: Although this row is in context for its income band, the pool behind it is thin and no unit isolates the practice cleanly. The Sumatran observation is a stated best case - plots lay close to remaining forest, and the regrowth is bundled with the earlier clearing and with seed proximity, with no share attributed to rewetting itself (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3); the Malaysian companion claim is an expected benefit rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). The Belarus gain fell short of its own target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent in the donor bogs for three years, and most of the prepared area was left to restore naturally (ev_wgy_blr_7); the Moldovan inventory is relayed by the project's own completion report with no numbers and no reference site (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The row therefore mixes tropical peat with temperate cut-over peat and a river-fed wetland, and says nothing measured about farmed landscapes or lower-income countries. No comparison with an intact reference and no recovery timescale is available here, so direction is all this supports; distance to intact forest or another seed source is the first site-level check, and a monitoring commitment should accompany any investment scoped on it.

effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping landscapes the benefit comes from adding aquatic habitat where almost none remains. Catchment-scale wetland creation benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness, with the accumulation curve still rising after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], and creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity in a landscape whose small waters had increased by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. conditionality: Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Sweden and Ohio, and neither is a restoration of a lost wetland: they are wetlands created under a programme designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5] and a pair of pumped experimental basins [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. The 30% figure is a design condition on habitat density, not a measured effect size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The Ohio comparison is planting against natural colonisation within created wetlands rather than wetland against no wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. Nothing here was measured in a tropical or low-income rainfed system, and no unit reports how the gain changes as the wetland ages.

effect_mechanism: Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat that the landscape has lost, and the new basins can reach the standard of the old ones. Dual-purpose created wetlands sustained alpha, beta and gamma diversity similar to that of natural lentic water bodies in the region [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2], and the pollution-sensitive stoneflies, mayflies and caddisflies made up almost twice as large a share of richness in the created wetlands, 19%, as in the reference ponds, 10% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. Catchment-scale creation benefited landscape biodiversity, particularly where aquatic habitat density rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each new wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness with no asymptote after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity where small waters had risen by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. effect_mechanism: Raising the water table and removing the degrading pressure is what allows peatland vegetation to re-establish, and adding an active revegetation step is what makes it quick. Enhanced restoration using moss-layer transfer brought Sphagnum cover towards, and potentially past, intact levels and reached intact-level specialist plant diversity within years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7); basic rewetting and tree felling produced marked recovery on a multi-decadal path (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2); and the systematic review's own summary is that active restoration or replacement measures are needed to speed recolonisation of bare peat (ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10). In Belarus, vegetation mapping after rewetting 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland found Phragmites-sedge communities on at least 398 ha, against no more than 20 ha at baseline (ev_wgy_blr_7). Where only the upper peat layer had been removed, biological structure recovered immediately (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10). On tropical peat the same lever appears as native peat-swamp-forest trees regrowing spontaneously in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
conditionality: Structure returning is not function returning, and neither is the same as matching an intact site. In restored peatlands, Sphagnum cover and peatland specialist cover remained well below intact peatlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1), and where biological structure did recover immediately the biogeochemical functioning of the same peatlands stayed statistically below reference decades later (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10) - so a row that reads as a biodiversity gain against a degraded baseline still carries a shortfall against the intact reference, and the comparisons must not be netted against each other. The restoration method decides whether there is any result at all within an investment horizon: passive restoration was projected over centuries (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5), with specialist cover stagnating or further deteriorating long after abandonment (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6), and stressor removal without revegetation appeared to cause a decline in specialist diversity, a response the authors could not predict reliably (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8). The Belarus result shows the same dependence on active work: it fell short of the target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent from the donor bogs for three years so only 70 ha were planted or sown, and reed and cattail were first to appear on the rest, expected to give way to sedge as the sites develop (ev_wgy_blr_7). The temperate and boreal evidence is substantial and mostly high-income; the tropical units are thin, bundled with clearing and seed proximity, and partly a stated potential rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4), so transferring this row to a tropical peat landscape rests on mechanism, not on matched evidence. A review of agricultural use of wetlands adds the other side of the ledger, what draining the existing peatland cost in the first place: agriculture in the Dutch wetlands, particularly in the past century, has been shown to be non-sustainable through subsidence and devastating for wetland biodiversity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_3), and agriculture on South-East Asian tropical peat soils has resulted in irreversible biodiversity losses (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_4). The review ties both losses to intensive drained use (fertiliser, pesticides and deeper drainage for crops such as oil palm) rather than to drainage alone. These units describe the degraded state that rewetting starts from, not anything rewetting achieved, so they are carried as context and enter through the existing-wetland home-family route rather than as measured restoration outcomes; the word irreversible is a further warning that the gain above is a partial recovery, not a return of what was lost.

effect_mechanism: Reinstating hydrology on a degraded wetland puts back standing water and saturated soil, and the gain is measured against that degraded starting point. How degraded that point is comes from a review of agricultural use of wetlands, restating the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: natural wetlands reclaimed by drainage and land amelioration have lost much of their original character, leading to reduced biodiversity and reduced performance of functions other than crop productivity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_5). That unit describes what reclaiming an existing wetland cost, not a restoration result; it enters this family row through the existing-wetland home-family route, as a statement of the degraded starting point rather than a measured restoration outcome. Restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity overall and the diversity of vertebrates, vascular plants and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3). The mobile parts of the system return soonest: vertebrate assemblages reached reference structural values within a few years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6), and riverine and tidal wetlands kept connected by natural flow variation recovered biogeochemical function and biological structure after 20 and 30 years respectively (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9). Project cases show the same fast early response. After the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes, park reports cited by the World Bank record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50 (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1); a project-supported inventory found flora and fauna beginning to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland in Moldova was restored (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). A review of floodplain wetland restoration studies finds the same direction in how projects report themselves: most published studies deemed their restoration activities successful or partially successful, irrespective of the restoration activity performed (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1). The Lao and Sierra Leone units come from protecting existing wetlands rather than restoring them: in Lao PDR, designating fishery conservation zones was followed by an increase in native fish populations and more fish for local consumption (ev_wgy_lao_3), and at Sierra Leone's Mamunta Mayosso sanctuary positive changes in biodiversity conservation are confirmed after cattle settlements were banned (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1).
conditionality: A restored wetland that falls short of an intact one is a recovery note, not harm, and it is kept apart from the gain above. The slow parts lag: plant assemblages took decades to converge statistically with reference sites and their absolute structural values remained below reference even 100 years after restoration, with biological structure and biogeochemical functioning still lower than reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), while inland depressional wetlands fed only by precipitation or groundwater had not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). The global syntheses disagree on whether that shortfall persists, since biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2). Not every group responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4). The project units are weaker than their numbers suggest. The Bulgarian counts are park reports taken within months of the first flooding (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2), and the Moldovan result is direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The floodplain review is a vote count of authors' own declared success against indicators they chose, not a measured effect against a baseline, and its authors warn that unsuccessful outcomes are likely under-reported (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1); it also relays a before-and-after study in which hydrological restoration of inundation levels failed to restore invertebrate food sources for birds, likely because of vague aims and predictions of what the target species required (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_2). The Sierra Leone claim is an evaluator's assertion about a bundle of grazing by-laws, boundary demarcation and co-management, and it depended on the exit of all Fula settlements and their cattle, a livelihood cost the biodiversity gain does not show (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1). The Lao result rests on project fish-monitoring records inside protected zones (ev_wgy_lao_3). The comparisons against intact reference sites (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9) are held out of the class for that reason: they measure how far recovery has to go, not what restoration adds over the degraded starting point.

The slow parts lag: plant assemblages took decades to converge statistically with reference sites and their absolute structural values remained below reference even 100 years after restoration, with biological structure and biogeochemical functioning still lower than reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), while inland depressional wetlands fed only by precipitation or groundwater had not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). The global syntheses disagree on whether that shortfall persists, since biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2). Not every group responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4). The project units are weaker than their numbers suggest. The Bulgarian counts are park reports taken within months of the first flooding (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2), and the Moldovan result is direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The floodplain review is a vote count of authors' own declared success against indicators they chose, not a measured effect against a baseline, and its authors warn that unsuccessful outcomes are likely under-reported (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1); it also relays a before-and-after study in which hydrological restoration of inundation levels failed to restore invertebrate food sources for birds, likely because of vague aims and predictions of what the target species required (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_2). The Lao result rests on project fish-monitoring records inside protected zones (ev_wgy_lao_3). The comparisons against intact reference sites (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9) are held out of the class for that reason: they measure how far recovery has to go, not what restoration adds over the degraded starting point.

effect_mechanism: Only units that weigh carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide together can say which way the balance falls. Where they state one they favour rewetting over keeping the peat drained, along a time path, and almost all of those net balances come from drained peatland. That is the sub-practice where the gain is clearest; across wetland management as a whole it is slight. On a hundred-year global warming potential basis, rewetting drained organic soils gives net annual removals of carbon dioxide in the majority of organic soil classes, an increase in annual methane, a decrease in nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon, and a lowering of net greenhouse-gas emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; the same authors restate that rewetting strongly increases methane yet in general represents a significant climate-change mitigation action because of the considerable decrease in carbon dioxide and the accompanying nitrous-oxide reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_3]. The time path is the point to carry forward. The peatland-rewetting question-and-answer document, citing the literature, states that rewetting initially causes a slight warming impact because of increased methane, but that in the longer term the result is cooling [ev_wgy_qa_3, ev_wgy_qa_4]; the Ramsar technical report, also citing studies, holds that even where rewetting produces a disproportionally large initial methane peak the longer-term climate effects are much better than maintaining the drained status quo [ev_wgy_ram_3], and that the combined fluxes of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon are very positive for the climate compared with the former drained situation [ev_wgy_ram_1]. Scenario modelling traces the same path through radiative forcing: methane forcing does not undermine the mitigation potential of rewetting, while postponing it increases long-term warming through continued carbon dioxide emission [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_3]; total forcing reaches a plateau soon after rewetting because carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide are halted and methane is short-lived in the atmosphere [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_4]; the methane cost may temporarily be substantial but the carbon dioxide cost of inaction is much higher [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_5]; and the warming from methane plus nitrous oxide is fully compensated by carbon dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3], with cumulative reductions of 583.8 and 782 tCO2eq per hectare under the modelled rewetting scenarios [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1]. Field-based rates tie the balance to the water table: every 10 cm reduction in effective water-table depth reduces the net warming impact of carbon dioxide plus methane by at least 3 t CO2e per hectare per year until the depth is less than 30 cm [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1], and between 5 and 13 cm the cooling from carbon dioxide sequestration exceeds the warming from methane on a hundred-year horizon [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. A German study cited in a Scottish evidence assessment found 17 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 saved by rewetting a reed-canary-grass peatland compared with its drained state, with no significant short-term effect of biomass harvest [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_1]; and a mesonetwork of restored wetlands on drained Californian peat showed that conversion can yield a net greenhouse-gas benefit over the original land use, but only in some cases [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. Behind those balances sit the parts of the ledger. Both advocacy-adjacent documents assert the gas exchange plainly: rewetting stops carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide but re-installs methane [ev_wgy_qa_1, ev_wgy_qa_2], and will always lead to a reinstatement of methane emissions [ev_wgy_ram_2]. While the water table stays below the surface, emissions from peat oxidation fall roughly linearly as it is raised, so roughly half of them can be avoided by raising the table to half its former depth — a statement about the oxidation term alone, not the methane that appears near the surface [ev_wgy_ram_4]. Restoration also rebuilds stocks: aboveground biomass (SMD 2.52), belowground biomass (1.94) and soil carbon (0.62) rose, with carbon dioxide flux falling significantly (SMD −0.43) while methane rose (0.44) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_2]. A global meta-analysis of wetland carbon budgets reads the time path from the restoration year rather than from the drained state: the switchover from net warming to net cooling for restored freshwater marsh, restored peatlands and rewetted peatlands comes after 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. German inventory and agency sources, cited in an economic assessment, put the saving from raising the water level on drained organic soils at an average of 20-35 t CO2e per hectare per year for arable land and grassland [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1]. Soil carbon concentration points the same way against degraded sites: restored wetlands had 30% higher soil organic carbon than paired degraded wetlands (RR: 0.26) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_1], with restored inland wetlands significantly higher (RR: 0.78) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_4]. The other sub-practices add parts of the ledger rather than net balances. Planted salt marsh increased soil organic carbon stocks by on average 10.70 Mg C/ha with respect to adjacent degraded wetlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6], a stock gain with no gas term. In created wetlands, methane emission rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, while nitrous oxide fluxes were lower when marsh and edge plots were inundated [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on peat extraction sites caused methane emissions yet had potential to reduce greenhouse-gas fluxes through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9].
conditionality: The class follows the sub-practice vote. Only the peatland family reads moderate, because the modelled and field net balances for rewetting drained peat sit there. The coastal, creation and restoration-rewetting families each read slight, so the roll-up is slight, although the pooled evidence alone read moderate. The restoration-rewetting family carries the decadal net-warming finding below, and the coastal and creation families rest mostly on single-gas or stock units. A single-gas unit never sets this class: only a net carbon dioxide equivalent balance does. The horizon decides the sign, and a net balance in this row points against the climate on the short horizon: counted from the restoration year, all restored wetlands in the carbon-budget meta-analysis had a net warming effect, because of their relatively young age and the impossibility for methane emissions to equilibrate in the atmosphere, so restored wetlands do not directly mitigate radiative warming at the yearly to decadal time-scale, even though they can accumulate carbon in their soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1]; they turn to net cooling only after 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. That accounting does not net in the carbon dioxide the drained site would have gone on emitting - the same paper notes that while restored and rewetted wetlands re-establish methane emissions, rewetting also stops the high carbon dioxide emissions of the drained period [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_2] - so it measures the restored wetland as a new sink, not against the drained counterfactual the gains above use. The switchover range assumes steady fluxes and covers only sites that take up carbon dioxide at all. Both readings hold: against continued drainage rewetting is favoured; as a climate benefit a project can claim within its own lifetime, it is not. Water-table depth, climate zone and horizon decide whether the balance is a gain at all, and the methane term is where it turns. Where average water levels are raised above the peat surface, the net warming from higher methane is likely to exceed the cooling from the extra carbon dioxide sequestration over shorter time-horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]: raising the water table from 30 to 0 cm adds roughly 7 t CO2e per hectare per year of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], whereas stopping at 30 cm below the surface has a negligible influence on methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3], and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface is offered as the design that prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Climate zone splits the answer: in the tropics the cooling is immediate and almost linearly increasing because the methane rise offsets only a few per cent of it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], while in temperate and boreal agricultural peat the methane offsets a major part of the cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4], and on forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling from reduced carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide for at least the first 40 years, and at least 50% even 100 years after rewetting [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5]; higher emissions were even estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts, which the authors call an apparent anomaly of their disaggregation [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]. Timing matters as much as place: carbon dioxide emissions decline soon after restoration whereas methane typically rises in the short term, with emerging evidence that the increase weakens as the ecosystem matures [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_11], individual studies report a methane peak in the first years [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6], and in seagrass the only significant response to restoration was an increase in methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]. Even the global scenario that maximises mitigation nets out small: optimal re-wetting of peat cropland and grassland generates net carbon dioxide uptake of 106 Mt per year against an offsetting 91 Mt of methane, leaving a small net removal [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6], while the less ambitious option of halving drainage depths cuts present-day carbon dioxide plus methane emissions by 65% [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7]. The prior land use splits the answer as well: the Ramsar report, citing studies, states that rewetting tropical peat and agricultural peat outside the tropics always has a large and rapid mitigation effect, but that on boreal forestry-drained peat the effect may be much lower and slower, complicated by changing albedo and by substantial carbon dioxide emissions after clear-cutting [ev_wgy_ram_5]. Paludiculture and permanence carry their own limits. The 25-30 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 reduction quoted for paludiculture is mostly avoided emissions from deep-drained peat cropland, and the same assessment records that field experiments disagree on whether paludiculture sites become a net carbon dioxide sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_2]. Harvesting Sphagnum biomass is judged likely to prevent the peat from being a long-term carbon store and to cause further peat degradation — a review judgement, not a measurement, but a reversal for that form of paludiculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_3]. Converting rewetted peat back to agriculture is estimated to release 6.5 t C ha-1 yr-1 of additional emissions, a carbon-only figure for the loss side of the ledger [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_4]. And restored freshwater marshes that accrete soil carbon do so at the cost of significant methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4]. Two further limits belong on this row. First, the strength rests on modelled scenarios rather than on measured net balances, and several units describe a single gas or a programme total and cannot carry a net claim. The Belarus terminal evaluation estimates emissions of 7.1 tons per ha per year after rewetting and 4.9 after 20 years, and reports a 65 % reduction against baseline with 75 % anticipated after 20 years; the evaluation calls these greenhouse-gas emissions, but the estimates are carbon dioxide only, no methane is reported, and they are modelled, so they describe the carbon dioxide part of the ledger, not a net balance [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]. Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency attributes a reduction of approximately 285 million tons of CO2eq to water-management improvement, derived from a water-level monitoring database rather than from measured fluxes [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1]. The measured units are mostly single-gas: restoration decreased soil carbon dioxide emission and increased methane against the unrestored extraction site, both rising with a higher water table and more vascular plant cover [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2]; a British gully-blocking restoration changed neither photosynthesis nor ecosystem respiration while methane was significantly greater in the sparsely vegetated rewetted pans [ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null, ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up]; and in Sumatra the carbon case is read off subsidence, halved where water tables were raised, implying an emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1]. Further single-gas or national figures join them: groundwater held at 0.4 m is cited as cutting subsidence and emissions by 25%-30% [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_3]; Indonesia's peat-restoration pathway could provide up to 171.6 MtCO2e a year nationally, but it is counted as carbon dioxide only, with no methane term [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_1]; and mangrove reforestation there is put at 8.9 MtCO2e a year, far less than avoided mangrove deforestation and degradation [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_2]. Each of those describes a part of the ledger, not the balance. The soil-carbon meta-analysis measures concentration, not stock, with no gas term, and splits by approach: passive restoration - farmland abandonment and grazing prohibition - showed 141% higher soil organic carbon, while active hydrological, plant and soil restoration was not significant in restoring it (8%, confidence interval spanning zero) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_3]; coastal wetlands showed no significant improvement [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_5]. The German 20-35 t CO2e figure is second-hand from emission-factor sources and the paper does not itself show the methane term [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1]. Second, a rewetted site is not an intact one: at an Irish rewetted peatland the carbon dioxide emission factor fell significantly but methane stayed above natural sites, and after a decade of rewetting the global warming potential of the rewetted sites was still higher than intact peatlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]. That is incomplete recovery against an intact reference; the gain claimed here is against the drained, degraded starting point, and on tropical plantation peat even full water-table control was modelled to cut emissions by no more than 20% of what drainage currently causes [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]. The country-bearing evidence is northern-European, Canadian, Irish, Estonian, Belarusian, Californian and Indonesian; the tropical results that carry the largest mitigation are modelled [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7].

That accounting does not net in the carbon dioxide the drained site would have gone on emitting - the same paper notes that while restored and rewetted wetlands re-establish methane emissions, rewetting also stops the high carbon dioxide emissions of the drained period [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_2] - so it measures the restored wetland as a new sink, not against the drained counterfactual the gains above use. The switchover range assumes steady fluxes and covers only sites that take up carbon dioxide at all. Both readings hold: against continued drainage rewetting is favoured; as a climate benefit a project can claim within its own lifetime, it is not. Water-table depth, climate zone and horizon decide whether the balance is a gain at all, and the methane term is where it turns. Where average water levels are raised above the peat surface, the net warming from higher methane is likely to exceed the cooling from the extra carbon dioxide sequestration over shorter time-horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]: raising the water table from 30 to 0 cm adds roughly 7 t CO2e per hectare per year of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], whereas stopping at 30 cm below the surface has a negligible influence on methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3], and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface is offered as the design that prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Climate zone splits the answer: in the tropics the cooling is immediate and almost linearly increasing because the methane rise offsets only a few per cent of it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], while in temperate and boreal agricultural peat the methane offsets a major part of the cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4], and on forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling from reduced carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide for at least the first 40 years, and at least 50% even 100 years after rewetting [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5]; higher emissions were even estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts, which the authors call an apparent anomaly of their disaggregation [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]. Timing matters as much as place: carbon dioxide emissions decline soon after restoration whereas methane typically rises in the short term, with emerging evidence that the increase weakens as the ecosystem matures [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_11], individual studies report a methane peak in the first years [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6], and in seagrass the only significant response to restoration was an increase in methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]. Even the global scenario that maximises mitigation nets out small: optimal re-wetting of peat cropland and grassland generates net carbon dioxide uptake of 106 Mt per year against an offsetting 91 Mt of methane, leaving a small net removal [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6], while the less ambitious option of halving drainage depths cuts present-day carbon dioxide plus methane emissions by 65% [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7]. The prior land use splits the answer as well: the Ramsar report, citing studies, states that rewetting tropical peat and agricultural peat outside the tropics always has a large and rapid mitigation effect, but that on boreal forestry-drained peat the effect may be much lower and slower, complicated by changing albedo and by substantial carbon dioxide emissions after clear-cutting [ev_wgy_ram_5]. Paludiculture and permanence carry their own limits. The 25-30 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 reduction quoted for paludiculture is mostly avoided emissions from deep-drained peat cropland, and the same assessment records that field experiments disagree on whether paludiculture sites become a net carbon dioxide sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_2]. Harvesting Sphagnum biomass is judged likely to prevent the peat from being a long-term carbon store and to cause further peat degradation — a review judgement, not a measurement, but a reversal for that form of paludiculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_3]. Converting rewetted peat back to agriculture is estimated to release 6.5 t C ha-1 yr-1 of additional emissions, a carbon-only figure for the loss side of the ledger [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_4]. And restored freshwater marshes that accrete soil carbon do so at the cost of significant methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4]. Two further limits belong on this row. First, the strength rests on modelled scenarios rather than on measured net balances, and several units describe a single gas or a programme total and cannot carry a net claim. The Belarus terminal evaluation estimates emissions of 7.1 tons per ha per year after rewetting and 4.9 after 20 years, and reports a 65 % reduction against baseline with 75 % anticipated after 20 years; the evaluation calls these greenhouse-gas emissions, but the estimates are carbon dioxide only, no methane is reported, and they are modelled, so they describe the carbon dioxide part of the ledger, not a net balance [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]. Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency attributes a reduction of approximately 285 million tons of CO2eq to water-management improvement, derived from a water-level monitoring database rather than from measured fluxes [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1]. The measured units are mostly single-gas: restoration decreased soil carbon dioxide emission and increased methane against the unrestored extraction site, both rising with a higher water table and more vascular plant cover [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2]; a British gully-blocking restoration changed neither photosynthesis nor ecosystem respiration while methane was significantly greater in the sparsely vegetated rewetted pans [ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null, ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up]; and in Sumatra the carbon case is read off subsidence, halved where water tables were raised, implying an emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1]. Further single-gas or national figures join them: groundwater held at 0.4 m is cited as cutting subsidence and emissions by 25%-30% [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_3]; Indonesia's peat-restoration pathway could provide up to 171.6 MtCO2e a year nationally, but it is counted as carbon dioxide only, with no methane term [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_1]; and mangrove reforestation there is put at 8.9 MtCO2e a year, far less than avoided mangrove deforestation and degradation [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_2]. Each of those describes a part of the ledger, not the balance. The soil-carbon meta-analysis measures concentration, not stock, with no gas term, and splits by approach: passive restoration - farmland abandonment and grazing prohibition - showed 141% higher soil organic carbon, while active hydrological, plant and soil restoration was not significant in restoring it (8%, confidence interval spanning zero) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_3]; coastal wetlands showed no significant improvement [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_5]. The German 20-35 t CO2e figure is second-hand from emission-factor sources and the paper does not itself show the methane term [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1]. Second, a rewetted site is not an intact one: at an Irish rewetted peatland the carbon dioxide emission factor fell significantly but methane stayed above natural sites, and after a decade of rewetting the global warming potential of the rewetted sites was still higher than intact peatlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]. That is incomplete recovery against an intact reference; the gain claimed here is against the drained, degraded starting point, and on tropical plantation peat even full water-table control was modelled to cut emissions by no more than 20% of what drainage currently causes [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]. The country-bearing evidence is northern-European, Canadian, Irish, Estonian, Belarusian, Californian and Indonesian; the tropical results that carry the largest mitigation are modelled [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7].

effect_mechanism: In the humid tropics every unit in this pool is one side of the greenhouse-gas ledger, and no source weighs the sides against each other. On the carbon dioxide side, rewetting drained tropical peat slows subsidence and the peat decomposition it indicates [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1], with a stated ceiling on what in-plantation water management can buy back [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1] and a drained-forest case where raising the water level hardly reduced the surface flux because root respiration dominates [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]. effect_mechanism: This row rests on the drainage side of the ledger: it is mostly an account of the carbon that drained wetlands lose, and of the expectation that putting the water back stops the loss. Drained peatlands release 645 Mt C per year through soil respiration, approximately 5% of global annual anthropogenic carbon emissions [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release], and the driver is the water table itself — its decline stimulated heterotrophic rather than autotrophic soil respiration and was associated with an increase in subsidence rate, a relationship that held across climate zones and land uses [ev_wetflA_ma_wt_respiration]. The loss is largest where the peat is warm: drained tropical peatlands under different land uses respire an estimated 10,865 to 23,685 kg C per hectare per year, the highest of any zone or land use in that synthesis [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates], and degraded peatlands as a whole emit 2 Gt CO2 per year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. Reversing the driver is where the positive direction comes from: restoring degraded hydric soils and ecosystems is given a high potential for sequestering soil carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2], because carbon storage is enhanced under the anoxic conditions that flooded wetlands restore, which favour the accretion of organic matter [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3], and compared to degraded sites restored peatlands have lower carbon emission rates and over time can become net carbon sinks [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1].
conditionality: Nothing in this row weighs methane against carbon dioxide, so it cannot say what the net greenhouse-gas balance of rewetting is, or over what horizon. The units are either loss-frame estimates of what drainage costs or statements of sequestration potential, and the restoration-side units are expert and review assertions rather than measured rates: a high potential, an anoxic mechanism, and a direction of travel over unspecified time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3, ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1]. Scarcely any of the same-direction units say how big the effect is, which is why the row states a direction and not a size. The tropical rate is the rate of loss under drainage, not a measured recovery after rewetting [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates], and the global totals are not per-hectare effect sizes for an investment [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release, ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. The scope is the pooled, multi-country evidence rather than any named country, so there is no national or agro-ecological context attached to it; treat it as the carbon-dioxide and soil-carbon side of the case, to be read alongside the rows that carry the methane term.

effect_mechanism: Coastal restoration works through carbon stocks rather than through the peat gas balance. Planting salt marsh increased soil carbon storage against degraded wetlands (effect size 0.21), alongside gains in shoreline protection, primary productivity, biodiversity and fishery production [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], and raised soil organic carbon stocks by 10.70 +/- 3.45 Mg C per hectare relative to adjacent degraded wetlands, with aboveground and belowground biomass up 237.88 and 479.18 g per square metre [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. Measured against a natural marsh rather than a degraded baseline, restored marshes matched the reference on carbon dioxide flux (Hedges' g* = 0.03, n = 86, not significant) and on soil organic carbon accumulation rate (64.26 against 64.72 g per square metre per year, n = 18), and emitted significantly less methane (g* = -0.21, n = 70) [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. The unit that weighs both gases explains why coastal marsh differs from freshwater rewetting: mangroves and saltmarshes were the only two wetland types that were still net negative, because of the limited methane emissions generated in coastal wetlands in comparison with the magnitude of carbon dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_5].

Among wetland types, seagrass showed only a significant increase in methane flux, with no offsetting significant benefit, in a preprint whose own authors note that seagrass beds were under-represented and that tropical and southern regions are a major geographical gap [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]; seagrass and salt marsh are not interchangeable, and the only methane result in salt marsh points the other way [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. A second soil-carbon meta-analysis found that restored coastal wetlands showed no significant improvement in soil organic carbon over degraded ones (RR: 0.05; 95% CI: -0.08 to 0.19), in a pool that includes mangroves [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_5]. Indonesia's national figure for mangrove reforestation, 8.9 MtCO2e a year and far less than avoided mangrove deforestation and degradation, is cited second-hand, counts carbon dioxide only, and concerns mangroves rather than the marshes this family covers [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_2]. Comparator matters too: the salt-marsh stock gains are measured against degraded wetland, which is the counterfactual a restoration project faces [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6], while the equivalence results are measured against natural marsh and say that restored marshes accumulate carbon as fast as natural ones even while their stocks lag [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11]. justification.mechanism: Coastal restoration works through carbon stocks rather than through the peat gas balance. Planting salt marsh increased soil carbon storage against degraded wetlands (effect size 0.21), alongside gains in shoreline protection, primary productivity, biodiversity and fishery production [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], and raised soil organic carbon stocks by 10.70 +/- 3.45 Mg C per hectare relative to adjacent degraded wetlands, with aboveground and belowground biomass up 237.88 and 479.18 g per square metre [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. Measured against a natural marsh rather than a degraded baseline, restored marshes matched the reference on carbon dioxide flux (Hedges' g* = 0.03, n = 86, not significant) and on soil organic carbon accumulation rate (64.26 against 64.72 g per square metre per year, n = 18), and emitted significantly less methane (g* = -0.21, n = 70) [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. The unit that weighs both gases explains why coastal marsh differs from freshwater rewetting: mangroves and saltmarshes were the only two wetland types that were still net negative, because of the limited methane emissions generated in coastal wetlands in comparison with the magnitude of carbon dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_5].
justification.conditionality: The direction of this row rests on that single unit, and it is not a restoration result: it is the carbon budget of existing saltmarsh, from a meta-analysis that captured only two empirical saltmarsh studies [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_5]. Everything measured on restored coastal wetland here is a single gas or a stock and cannot set a class. Among wetland types, seagrass showed only a significant increase in methane flux, with no offsetting significant benefit, in a preprint whose own authors note that seagrass beds were under-represented and that tropical and southern regions are a major geographical gap [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]; seagrass and salt marsh are not interchangeable, and the only methane result in salt marsh points the other way [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. A second soil-carbon meta-analysis found that restored coastal wetlands showed no significant improvement in soil organic carbon over degraded ones (RR: 0.05; 95% CI: -0.08 to 0.19), in a pool that includes mangroves [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_5]. Indonesia's national figure for mangrove reforestation, 8.9 MtCO2e a year and far less than avoided mangrove deforestation and degradation, is cited second-hand, counts carbon dioxide only, and concerns mangroves rather than the marshes this family covers [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_2]. Comparator matters too: the salt-marsh stock gains are measured against degraded wetland, which is the counterfactual a restoration project faces [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6], while the equivalence results are measured against natural marsh and say that restored marshes accumulate carbon as fast as natural ones even while their stocks lag [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11]. The salt-marsh evidence is high-income and overwhelmingly North American, European and East Asian, with planting dominated by a single genus, and some plantings also received fertiliser or protective structures [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. No unit states a net balance for a restored coastal wetland over a stated horizon.

effect_mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on former peat-extraction sites had the potential to reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. Methane emission from vegetated areas rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions to the atmosphere even as they offered a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does: in the upland plots, fluxes did not differ between flooded and dry periods [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Because the register has no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide gains and the methane rise from the same experiment enter the pool with opposite signs, which makes the evidence look more divided than it is: both sources report a net gain with a methane penalty inside it. The row rests on a pair of pumped experimental basins in temperate Ohio and a review of boreal and northern European peat-extraction after-use. No unit states a net balance over any horizon, none measures how the balance changes as the created wetland matures, and none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].

effect_mechanism: On peat, the units that weigh all the gases together set the direction, and where they state a horizon they favour rewetting over the drained state, along a time path. On a hundred-year global warming potential basis, rewetting drained organic soils gives net annual removals of carbon dioxide in most soil classes, an increase in annual methane, a decrease in nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon, and a lowering of net greenhouse-gas emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_4]; every 10 cm the effective water-table depth is raised cuts the net warming of carbon dioxide plus methane by at least 3 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 until the table is within 30 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1], and between 5 and 13 cm depth the carbon dioxide cooling exceeds the methane warming [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. Other sources refuse a fixed horizon and report radiative forcing through time, finding that it plateaus soon after rewetting because carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide stop while the methane is short-lived, so the methane forcing does not undermine the mitigation and the carbon dioxide cost of delay is much higher [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_5]. The question-and-answer document on peatland rewetting, citing the literature, states that rewetting initially causes a slight warming impact because of increased methane, but that in the longer term the result is cooling [ev_wgy_qa_3, ev_wgy_qa_4]; the Ramsar technical report, also citing studies, holds that the combined fluxes of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon are very positive for the climate compared with the former drained situation [ev_wgy_ram_1], and that even after a disproportionally large initial methane peak the longer-term effects are much better than maintaining the drained status quo [ev_wgy_ram_3]. A German study cited in a Scottish evidence assessment found 17 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 saved by rewetting a reed-canary-grass peatland compared with its drained state [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_1], and German inventory and agency sources cited in an economic assessment put the saving from raising the water level on drained organic soils at an average of 20-35 t CO2e per hectare per year for arable land and grassland [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1]. The size of the prize is set by what drainage is already costing. Water-table decline stimulates heterotrophic rather than autotrophic soil respiration and raises the subsidence rate across climate zones and land uses [ev_wetflA_ma_wt_respiration]; drained peatlands release 645 Mt C yr-1 through soil respiration, about 5% of global annual anthropogenic carbon emissions [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release], the per-hectare losses highest in the drained tropics at 10,865 to 23,685 kg C ha-1 yr-1 [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates]; degraded peat emits 2 Gt CO2 a year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions and up more than 25% since 1990 [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]; and tropical peat drained for plantation lost an average 100 t CO2eq ha-1 yr-1 over 25 yr, 178 in the first 5 yr [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_2]. A review of agricultural use of wetlands states the same switch in general terms: drainage of peatlands results in peat oxidation, causing major subsidence as well as the switch of peatland systems from carbon sinks to major carbon sources [ev_carbon_sequestration_verh09_2]; and, restating an earlier estimate, it puts emissions from Indonesian drained peatlands alone at 516 megatonnes of carbon per year, fires excluded [ev_carbon_sequestration_verh09_1]. Both describe what draining the existing peatland costs, not what rewetting recovers, and both count carbon dioxide only, the second as a national total rather than a per-hectare rate, so they are carried as context for the size of the drained-state loss and enter through the existing-wetland home-family route rather than as measured restoration outcomes. Rewetting reverses the aerobic decomposition but re-establishes methane, and both gases have to be named [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1]. Both advocacy-adjacent documents assert the same exchange: rewetting stops carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide but re-installs methane [ev_wgy_qa_1, ev_wgy_qa_2, ev_wgy_ram_2]; and while the table stays below the surface, peat-oxidation emissions fall roughly linearly as it is raised, so roughly half can be avoided by raising it to half its former depth — the oxidation term only [ev_wgy_ram_4]. The peatland subgroup of a restoration meta-analysis shows the same shape, with significant increases in above- and belowground biomass and soil carbon and significant carbon dioxide flux reductions [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_7]. In the tropics the measured route is subsidence: canal blocking halved it where water tables rose from about -0.6 m to about -0.3 m [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2], implying a carbon emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in the well-rewetted area [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1], and dams can permanently raise the water table in a degraded peat dome, which reduces subsidence and carbon dioxide emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1].
conditionality: What the peat was drained for decides the net result. The Ramsar report, citing studies, states that rewetting tropical peat and agricultural peat outside the tropics always has a large and rapid mitigation effect, while on boreal forestry-drained peat the effect may be much lower and slower, complicated by albedo change and by carbon dioxide emissions after clear-cutting [ev_wgy_ram_5], in line with the forestry-drained results below. On tropical cropland and plantation peat, rewetting caused an immediate, almost linearly increasing cooling, the rising methane offsetting only a few per cent of the cooling from falling carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3]. On temperate and boreal agricultural peat the methane warming offsets a major part of that cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4]. On forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling for at least the first 40 years and still at least 50% a century later, so rewetting there warms over the policy-relevant horizon, and it also decreases the carbon stored in the trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_1]. Water above the peat surface is the other reversal: raising average water levels above the surface is likely to make the methane warming exceed the carbon dioxide cooling over shorter horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; taking the table from 30 cm depth to the surface adds about 7 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], where stopping at 30 cm has a negligible effect, at most 0.3 [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3]; and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Paludiculture and permanence add reversals: the 25-30 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 reduction quoted for paludiculture is mostly avoided emissions from deep-drained cropland, and field experiments disagree on whether such sites become a net carbon dioxide sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_2]; harvesting Sphagnum biomass is judged likely to prevent the peat from being a long-term carbon store and to cause further degradation, a review judgement rather than a measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_3]; and converting rewetted peat back to agriculture is estimated to release 6.5 t C ha-1 yr-1, a carbon-only loss figure [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_4]. The remaining reversals are kept rather than averaged away: higher emissions were estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]; a rewetted Irish peatland emitted more methane than natural sites and its global warming potential was still above intact peatland after a decade, even though its carbon dioxide emission factor had fallen significantly to 104 g CO2-C m-2 yr-1 [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; a fertilised reed-canary-grass plot on cutover peat emitted 21,938 kg CO2 ha-1 yr-1 against 8,448 from the natural bog, although the same plots emitted far less methane than the bog and had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]; an upland English rewetting raised methane significantly in the sparsely vegetated pans while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not move, so nothing on the carbon dioxide side offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up, ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]; cutaway-peat restoration cut soil carbon dioxide emission and raised methane together, and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance and higher sensitivity to climate anomalies than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]; a methane peak in the first years after rewetting has been reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6]; and the peatland subgroup records methane rising significantly alongside its carbon dioxide and stock benefits [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_8]. Much of the apparent disagreement here is between gases rather than between findings: single-gas units are parts of the ledger, so a carbon dioxide fall and a methane rise taken from the same sentence enter with opposite signs [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]; and the one recovery-shortfall unit says peatland biogeochemical function remained statistically lower than reference wetlands 30 y after restoration, which is a statement about rebuilding an intact peatland, not about losing carbon against the drained baseline [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_11]. Programme totals and single-gas figures cannot carry a net claim: the Belarus terminal evaluation's per-hectare estimates of 7.1 tons per year after rewetting and 4.9 after 20 years, reported as a 65 % reduction with 75 % anticipated after 20 years, are carbon dioxide only with no methane reported, and modelled [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]; Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency attributes approximately 285 million tons of CO2eq of reduction to water management on the strength of a water-level monitoring database, not measured fluxes [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1]; Indonesia's national peat-restoration pathway of up to 171.6 MtCO2e a year counts carbon dioxide only, with no methane term [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_1]; and the 25%-30% cut in subsidence and emissions cited for groundwater held at 0.4 m is a subsidence-based carbon dioxide estimate, second-hand [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_3]. The German 20-35 t CO2e figure is also second-hand, from emission-factor sources, and the paper does not itself show the methane term [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1]. The tropical evidence is the thinnest and the most investable. The tropical rewetting scenarios rest on default emission factors [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], and the source of those factors states plainly that no studies exist on rewetted tropical sites with the water table close to the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; the tropical rows of the water-table synthesis are extrapolated from temperate and boreal relationships rather than measured [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6]. Measured tropical results are muted: a year after canal damming in Central Kalimantan, carbon dioxide emissions were 7305 then 7444 g m-2 yr-1 at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, read by the authors as no marked response [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site stayed a weak methane source and the source grew [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3] while the forest floor stayed a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]; higher water tables had a relatively small effect on annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]; raising the groundwater level hardly reduces peat-surface carbon dioxide flux in drained forest, because root respiration dominates it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]; regrowth on open restored areas is still too small to compensate peat decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3]; the higher water tables did not completely compensate the increased subsidence near the canals [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5]; canal blocking is a long-term measure that works through vegetation regeneration rather than on its own [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6]; inside a drained plantation that stays in production the ceiling is a reduction of no more than 20% [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]; and the Southeast Asian reviews call the outcomes inconclusive, with decomposition continuing in the saturated zone and carbon leaving as methane or through fluvial networks, so a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural one in its gas exchange [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2]. The remaining tropical claim is a direction-only review line about a bundled rewetting and fire-prevention programme, with no magnitude and no comparator [ev_carbon_sequestration_alex26_2], beside general statements of potential [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_9].
