Both describe what draining the existing peatland costs, not what rewetting recovers, and both count carbon dioxide only, the second as a national total rather than a per-hectare rate, so they are carried as context for the size of the drained-state loss and enter through the existing-wetland home-family route rather than as measured restoration outcomes. Rewetting reverses the aerobic decomposition but re-establishes methane, and both gases have to be named [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1]. Both advocacy-adjacent documents assert the same exchange: rewetting stops carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide but re-installs methane [ev_wgy_qa_1, ev_wgy_qa_2, ev_wgy_ram_2]; and while the table stays below the surface, peat-oxidation emissions fall roughly linearly as it is raised, so roughly half can be avoided by raising it to half its former depth — the oxidation term only [ev_wgy_ram_4]. The peatland subgroup of a restoration meta-analysis shows the same shape, with significant increases in above- and belowground biomass and soil carbon and significant carbon dioxide flux reductions [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_7]. In the tropics the measured route is subsidence: canal blocking halved it where water tables rose from about -0.6 m to about -0.3 m [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2], implying a carbon emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in the well-rewetted area [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1], and dams can permanently raise the water table in a degraded peat dome, which reduces subsidence and carbon dioxide emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1].
justification.conditionality: What the peat was drained for decides the net result. The Ramsar report, citing studies, states that rewetting tropical peat and agricultural peat outside the tropics always has a large and rapid mitigation effect, while on boreal forestry-drained peat the effect may be much lower and slower, complicated by albedo change and by carbon dioxide emissions after clear-cutting [ev_wgy_ram_5], in line with the forestry-drained results below. On tropical cropland and plantation peat, rewetting caused an immediate, almost linearly increasing cooling, the rising methane offsetting only a few per cent of the cooling from falling carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3]. On temperate and boreal agricultural peat the methane warming offsets a major part of that cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4]. On forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling for at least the first 40 years and still at least 50% a century later, so rewetting there warms over the policy-relevant horizon, and it also decreases the carbon stored in the trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_1]. Water above the peat surface is the other reversal: raising average water levels above the surface is likely to make the methane warming exceed the carbon dioxide cooling over shorter horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; taking the table from 30 cm depth to the surface adds about 7 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], where stopping at 30 cm has a negligible effect, at most 0.3 [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3]; and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Paludiculture and permanence add reversals: the 25-30 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 reduction quoted for paludiculture is mostly avoided emissions from deep-drained cropland, and field experiments disagree on whether such sites become a net carbon dioxide sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_2]; harvesting Sphagnum biomass is judged likely to prevent the peat from being a long-term carbon store and to cause further degradation, a review judgement rather than a measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_3]; and converting rewetted peat back to agriculture is estimated to release 6.5 t C ha-1 yr-1, a carbon-only loss figure [ev_carbon_sequestration_cxc_4]. The remaining reversals are kept rather than averaged away: higher emissions were estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]; a rewetted Irish peatland emitted more methane than natural sites and its global warming potential was still above intact peatland after a decade, even though its carbon dioxide emission factor had fallen significantly to 104 g CO2-C m-2 yr-1 [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; a fertilised reed-canary-grass plot on cutover peat emitted 21,938 kg CO2 ha-1 yr-1 against 8,448 from the natural bog, although the same plots emitted far less methane than the bog and had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]; an upland English rewetting raised methane significantly in the sparsely vegetated pans while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not move, so nothing on the carbon dioxide side offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up, ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]; cutaway-peat restoration cut soil carbon dioxide emission and raised methane together, and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance and higher sensitivity to climate anomalies than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]; a methane peak in the first years after rewetting has been reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6]; and the peatland subgroup records methane rising significantly alongside its carbon dioxide and stock benefits [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_8]. Much of the apparent disagreement here is between gases rather than between findings: single-gas units are parts of the ledger, so a carbon dioxide fall and a methane rise taken from the same sentence enter with opposite signs [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]; and the one recovery-shortfall unit says peatland biogeochemical function remained statistically lower than reference wetlands 30 y after restoration, which is a statement about rebuilding an intact peatland, not about losing carbon against the drained baseline [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_11]. Programme totals and single-gas figures cannot carry a net claim: the Belarus terminal evaluation's per-hectare estimates of 7.1 tons per year after rewetting and 4.9 after 20 years, reported as a 65 % reduction with 75 % anticipated after 20 years, are carbon dioxide only with no methane reported, and modelled [ev_wgy_blr_3, ev_wgy_blr_4]; Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency attributes approximately 285 million tons of CO2eq of reduction to water management on the strength of a water-level monitoring database, not measured fluxes [ev_carbon_sequestration_cifor270_1]; Indonesia's national peat-restoration pathway of up to 171.6 MtCO2e a year counts carbon dioxide only, with no methane term [ev_wet_carbon_novi22_1]; and the 25%-30% cut in subsidence and emissions cited for groundwater held at 0.4 m is a subsidence-based carbon dioxide estimate, second-hand [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_3]. The tropical evidence is the thinnest and the most investable. Measured tropical results are muted: a year after canal damming in Central Kalimantan, carbon dioxide emissions were 7305 then 7444 g m-2 yr-1 at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, read by the authors as no marked response [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site stayed a weak methane source and the source grew [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3] while the forest floor stayed a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]; higher water tables had a relatively small effect on annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]; raising the groundwater level hardly reduces peat-surface carbon dioxide flux in drained forest, because root respiration dominates it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]; regrowth on open restored areas is still too small to compensate peat decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3]; the higher water tables did not completely compensate the increased subsidence near the canals [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5]; canal blocking is a long-term measure that works through vegetation regeneration rather than on its own [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6]; inside a drained plantation that stays in production the ceiling is a reduction of no more than 20% [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]; and the Southeast Asian reviews call the outcomes inconclusive, with decomposition continuing in the saturated zone and carbon leaving as methane or through fluvial networks, so a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural one in its gas exchange [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2]. effect_mechanism: The net balance comes first. Rewetting degraded wetlands at rates matching historical degradation cuts greenhouse-gas emissions by 583.8 to 782 t CO2eq ha-1 under its two scenarios [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1], of which carbon dioxide alone carries 77.6% in the all-rewetting case [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_2], and the radiative forcing caused by methane and nitrous oxide is fully compensated by carbon dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3] — a volume equivalent to ten percent of anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_7]. The design target follows from the water-table gradient: the sum of all three gases is lowest, near zero, when the water table is near the ground surface, between -30 and -5 cm [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_4], against 19.7 and 11.2 t CO2eq ha-1 yr-1 from boreal and temperate wetlands held at or below -70 cm [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_6]. Measurements over a mesonetwork of restored wetlands on drained Californian peat showed that conversion can, in some cases, yield a net greenhouse-gas benefit compared with the original land use [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5], and a global carbon-budget meta-analysis finds restored freshwater marsh, restored peatlands and rewetted peatlands switching from net warming to net cooling after 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. Behind that balance sit the parts of the ledger. Pooled across restored and altered wetlands, carbon dioxide flux fell significantly (SMD -0.43; CI -0.84 to -0.01; k = 111) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1], soil carbon rose (SMD 0.62; CI 0.23 to 0.99; k = 207) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4], and aboveground and belowground biomass rose by the largest effect sizes in the analysis (SMD 2.52 and 1.94) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6], while nitrous oxide showed a non-significant trend towards reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_3]. Restoring degraded hydric soils is held to have a high potential for sequestrating soil carbon, because flooding restores the anoxic conditions optimal for accretion of organic matter [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3]. Soil carbon concentration also rises against the degraded state: restored wetlands had 30% higher soil organic carbon than paired degraded wetlands (RR: 0.26), passively restored ones 141% higher, and restored inland wetlands significantly higher (RR: 0.78) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_4].
conditionality: Several things pull against this row's direction, and none is a finding that rewetting releases more carbon than leaving the peat drained. The first is methane, a single-gas part of the ledger rather than a net balance: methane flux rose after restoration (SMD 0.44; CI 0.14 to 0.74; k = 95) [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_2], hydrological interventions specifically produced elevated methane alongside reduced nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_9], methane is maximal where water levels stand well above the soil surface and minimal where the table is well below it [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_5], and carbon dioxide emissions decline soon after restoration while methane typically rises in the short term, with emerging evidence that the rise weakens as the ecosystem matures [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_11]; restored freshwater marshes accrete soil carbon at the cost of significant methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4], and the same source's net statement holds only in some cases [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. Those are the methane halves of the very sentences whose carbon dioxide halves sit in the mechanism above, and the same sources conclude a net benefit [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3]. The second is the comparator: units measuring restored wetlands against intact reference wetlands rather than against the degraded baseline — soil carbon still 50% lower after 20 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_2], organic matter at 62% of reference at 20-30 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_3], biogeochemical function at 79% of reference at 30 y in temperate and 53% at 50 y in cold climates [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_13, ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_12], climate regulation the largest service shortfall against natural wetlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_meli14_6], and soil organic carbon in restored wetlands 38% below natural wetlands [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_6]. The third is a net balance on a different clock, and it is the measured harm in this row: counted from the restoration year, all restored wetlands in the carbon-budget meta-analysis had a net warming effect, because of their relatively young age and the impossibility for methane emissions to equilibrate in the atmosphere, so restored wetlands do not directly mitigate radiative warming at the yearly to decadal time-scale, even though they can accumulate carbon in their soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1]; cooling arrives only after 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. That accounting leaves out the drained-state carbon dioxide that rewetting stops - the same paper says rewetting re-establishes methane but also stops the high carbon dioxide emissions of the drained period [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_2] - and the switchover range assumes steady fluxes and covers only sites that take up carbon dioxide at all. So the slight positive here is a long-horizon, against-drainage reading; over a project's own lifetime a restored wetland counted as a new sink is net warming. Read together, the pool says rewetting cuts the net balance while raising methane, and that a rewetted site stays below an intact one for decades. Real limits remain. The near-zero optimum and the methane gradient are read across the water tables of existing wetlands rather than before and after at rewetted sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_6]. The meta-analysis is a preprint whose tropical and arid pairs are under-represented, with publication bias detected for the stock terms, so those effect sizes are likely inflated [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6]. The global scenarios are modelled projections, and no horizon is stated for the per-hectare figure [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_7]. The supporting gain statements are assertions of potential with no rate, country or climate zone attached [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3]. Nothing in this scope row is a measurement at a rewetted tropical site, and the prior land use that the tropical case turns on is not distinguished anywhere in this pool. The soil-carbon meta-analysis measures concentration, not stock, with no gas term, and active hydrological, plant and soil restoration was not significant in restoring soil organic carbon (8% higher, confidence interval spanning zero), while the passive gain may partly reflect less-degraded starting sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_2].

effect_mechanism: Across boreo-temperate wetlands, restoration — mostly ditch blocking in drained peatlands — increased groundwater levels by 22 [16, 28] cm near the intervention, whereas drainage caused a drawdown of 19 [10, 27] cm [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise]; because the effects of restoration and drainage were of similar magnitudes but opposite directions, rewetting of drained peatlands can on average be expected to restore groundwater levels near the ditch [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. Groundwater level is used here as a component of catchment water yield.
conditionality: The rise is local: it decreased exponentially with distance from the restored ditch and was reduced to 50% after 9 [5, 26] m, while 50% of the drainage drawdown remained at 21 [11, 64] m [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay], so restoration may not reach all the area affected by drainage, with a strong dependence on local context [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. The literature reporting groundwater measurements outside the wetland soil was too limited for a reliable evaluation, so effects beyond the wetland are inconclusive [ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]. No unit measures water leaving the catchment or reaching downstream users, and the evidence is a single meta-analysis of boreal and temperate wetlands in high-income countries, mostly ditch blocking in drained peatlands, so its relevance to a dryland farming system is untested.

effect_mechanism: Cost per hectare is set mainly by what the restoration has to build. Re-establishing water flows is the cheap end: Indonesia's national canal-blocking programme is estimated at US$2,300/ha [ev_wgy_ram_19] and peatland restoration there at an average of around USD1,866 ha-1 [ev_project_cost_alex26_1]; controlled flooding of former Danube marshes in Bulgaria came in at US$1,903/ha at completion against US$2,145/ha at appraisal [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1]; wetland revegetation in Vermont is costed at $3200 ha-1 against $6400 ha-1 for forest revegetation [ev_project_cost_gour20_5]. A systematic review of Indonesian valuation studies reports peatland restoration costs mostly between US$500 and US$2,500 per ha [ev_wet_cost_jali25_1]; within it, modelled figures are US$1625/ha for restoring degraded deep peat [ev_wet_cost_jali25_2], an average lowest direct cost of US$1,866/ha with opportunity costs left out [ev_wet_cost_jali25_3], and an assumed regulation cost of rewetting of US$1,725.93/ha [ev_wet_cost_jali25_6]; the only figures from projects actually carried out are gross costs of US$16-43/ha and US$313-450/ha in Central Kalimantan, depending on the level of challenge each project met [ev_wet_cost_jali25_4]. Planting and hard engineering are the expensive end: in the salt marsh review, hydrological restoration at unprotected middle-income sites cost 6,090 to 9,945 $/ha against 26,945 to 42,756 $/ha for vegetation restoration [ev_project_cost_wang22_3, ev_project_cost_wang22_4], and whole-project means run to 454,285 to 694,724 $/ha at unprotected high-income sites [ev_project_cost_wang22_2].
conditionality: No cost figure comes from a low- or lower-middle-income country, so these numbers orient rather than transfer. They are not comparable with each other: some are programme estimates with no price year (Indonesia), some exclude land (the Vermont easement is costed separately), and the salt marsh means are total project cost divided by small restored areas, including engineering and land. The Indonesian review figures are cited second-hand, mostly ex-ante, and converted to US dollars by the review authors; the ex-post Central Kalimantan costs are total gross cost divided by area, which the review notes are much lower than other studies, and indirect costs made up a large share of them [ev_wet_cost_jali25_4]. These are the only ex-post costs from a middle-income country in the pool. Read them ordinally: large-area hydrological rewetting sits in the low thousands of US dollars per hectare, small engineered coastal projects orders of magnitude higher. effect_mechanism: Every unit in this row comes from the same global salt-marsh review, which reports project budgets divided by the area restored. Mean total cost per hectare at unprotected sites is USD 495,067-876,564 in middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_1] and USD 454,285-694,724 in high-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_2]. Broken out by method, within the middle-income unprotected cell, hydrological restoration costs USD 6,090-9,945 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_3] while vegetation restoration costs USD 26,945-42,756 [ev_project_cost_wang22_4]. What a coastal project does therefore drives its cost far more than where it is done.
conditionality: A single source carries the whole row, so there is no cross-source check on it. The headline per-hectare totals are flagged by the compilers as implausibly high for a landscape intervention: project areas are small and the budgets include engineering, hard structures and land, so the ordinal reading (coastal restoration is expensive, and hydrological work is its cheapest component) is what transfers, not the number. The quoted ranges are the spread across the review's alternative monetary conversion methods, not confidence intervals. The evidence base is China, Great Britain, the Netherlands and the United States; it is not a low- or lower-middle-income cost, and tidal and marsh engineering costs should not be carried to inland or smallholder settings.

effect_mechanism: Restoration costs are pushed up by engineering, land and regulation rather than brought down: tidal reinstatement is described as more cost-intensive than other coastal restoration because it needs hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility work, spatial modelling and permits [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5]. Scale matters: Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta (128,000 ha) cost US$20.1 million, while a 38 ha US saltmarsh project cost US$1.17 million [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4]. For wet farming on rewetted peat, specialised harvesting equipment and adapted production raise investment cost and risk above the drained baseline [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3]; Sphagnum farming establishment, calculated from pilot cost data in 2011 and again in 2016, fell between the dates but stayed in the order of a hundred thousand euros per hectare of production field [ev_wgy_wich_7].
conditionality: The evidence is almost entirely high-income (US, European and Australian projects); nothing here shows restoration lowering farm or project costs. The Sphagnum figures fall between the two dates but stay far above conventional land use, and they are for a high-input pilot. Do not read the absence of cost-reduction evidence as proof that low-cost community-based rewetting in low-income settings cannot be cheap; it is simply not in the pool.

effect_mechanism: Wetlands store water in the wet season and release it slowly, sustaining river flow when the rain fails. In a distributed hydrological model of the Nenjiang basin, riparian wetlands overall alleviated drought [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2], and across most scenarios the loss of minimum flow and the increase in drought deficit from removing wetlands outweighed the gains, so the wetlands overall supported low flow during the severe drought of 2011 [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6].
conditionality: Type and position flip the sign: isolated wetlands could intensify the drought deficit to some extent, because water held away from the channel is lost to evaporation rather than sustaining low flow [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3]. All of the evidence is a single modelling study in temperate, upper-middle-income northeast China, and it works by deleting wetlands that already exist from the model rather than by restoring any, so it supports conserving wetlands more directly than building them [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. No magnitude is attached to the drought relief, nothing was measured in the field, and the water reaches users downstream rather than the land where the work is done.

effect_mechanism: What an establishment bill buys depends on the wetland type and on how much hydrological work it needs. In a large tropical peat rewetting trial, where dams are built in large volumes the construction cost per compacted-peat canal dam is estimated at about 300 US$, which the authors call very economical compared with rewetting methods using wood and other materials brought in from elsewhere [ev_project_cost_hooi24_4]. A global meta-analysis of restoration costs gives median total project costs per hectare per year of the restoration event, in 2010 US$: US$89 660 for saltmarsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6], US$71 221 for freshwater marsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_9], US$20 948 for floodplains [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_7] and US$1229 for peatlands [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_8]. Read ordinally, marsh restoration, which may need more hydrological manipulation such as weirs, is the expensive end and peatland rewetting the cheap end.
conditionality: The Taillardat per-hectare-per-year figures are TOTAL PROJECT costs, the capital of the restoration event annualised over its duration, not maintenance; that is why they sit in establishment cost and not recurrent cost (the cost-routing rule), and they must not be read as a yearly running bill. They are 2010 US$ medians over actual and planned projects. The dam figure is per structure, not per hectare; this source gives no basis for converting it to a per-hectare cost, and it has no stated currency year, so it cannot be put on the same scale as the medians. The saltmarsh and freshwater marsh projects behind the medians were all in high-income countries, the floodplain median rests on a single project and the peatland projects' countries are not stated; the only middle-income figure is the Indonesian dam cost. effect_mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). A systematic review adds an average flood peak reduction of 30% for river and floodplain management, a bundle of measures of which floodplain and wetland restoration is a part (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). On coastal marsh the evidence is a project record rather than a hydrograph: a review found that a sizeable proportion of salt-marsh and mangrove projects state improved protection from storm events (41% in salt-marshes and 50% in mangroves) (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
conditionality: The class follows the sub-practice vote, and it is moderate rather than strong. The strong result belongs to the peatland family: the largest measured peak cuts, 27% and 51% at re-vegetated and gully-blocked micro-catchments and 49% at a rewetted gully, come from restored upland peat (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow). The floodplain and wetland restoration family reads moderate: its modelled peak cuts are smaller, about 8% to 12% in the base case (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2), and it holds most of the reversals by position described below. The coastal family also reads moderate, resting on project-reported storm protection rather than measured flood peaks (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). The coastal and restoration families both read moderate, so the roll-up does too. The scoring applies to the hazard at the receptor, and that is where the evidence thins. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment in the best-monitored UK test (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null); the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null); monitoring cannot isolate a restoration effect from catchment storm-flow data (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable); and the evidence does not suggest a major difference to downstream flood risk at large catchment scales, or for the most extreme events (ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null). During major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated and the presence, absence or management of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The sign flips with position: an on-site storage gain can still increase flood peaks at catchment scale through flood-wave synchrony (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff partially synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); restoration at the wrong reach worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects and in some scenarios raised aggregate flood damages above the baseline (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); and moving the same project downstream along the channel turned a 14% peak reduction into about a 1% increase (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4). Rewetting also consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels for winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost). Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. The state-dependence statements (ev_wgy_ram_10, ev_wgy_ram_11, ev_wgy_ram_12) are guidance-level synthesis, two with their own references and one an expert assertion; they establish that the sign depends on the peat's starting state, on top of its catchment position, but not how often each case occurs. The 30% review average credits the whole river-and-floodplain bundle - river restoration, floodplain and wetland restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage - not wetland restoration alone; it is a peak, not a stage, figure from a corpus that is mostly European and largely British, and its statement that the reduction is larger in larger catchments sits against the catchment-scale nulls above (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Provenance: a temperate, high-income corpus of UK and US catchments almost without exception, with no measured low-income or lower-middle-income result in scope, and a benefit that reaches downstream receptors rather than the plot.

justification.mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). A systematic review adds an average flood peak reduction of 30% for river and floodplain management, a bundle of measures of which floodplain and wetland restoration is a part (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). On coastal marsh the evidence is a project record rather than a hydrograph: a review found that a sizeable proportion of salt-marsh and mangrove projects state improved protection from storm events (41% in salt-marshes and 50% in mangroves) (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
justification.conditionality: The class follows the sub-practice vote, and it is moderate rather than strong. The strong result belongs to the peatland family: the largest measured peak cuts, 27% and 51% at re-vegetated and gully-blocked micro-catchments and 49% at a rewetted gully, come from restored upland peat (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow). The floodplain and wetland restoration family reads moderate: its modelled peak cuts are smaller, about 8% to 12% in the base case (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2), and it holds most of the reversals by position described below. The coastal family also reads moderate, resting on project-reported storm protection rather than measured flood peaks (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). The coastal and restoration families both read moderate, so the roll-up does too. The scoring applies to the hazard at the receptor, and that is where the evidence thins. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment in the best-monitored UK test (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null); the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null); monitoring cannot isolate a restoration effect from catchment storm-flow data (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable); and the evidence does not suggest a major difference to downstream flood risk at large catchment scales, or for the most extreme events (ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null). During major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated and the presence, absence or management of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The sign flips with position: an on-site storage gain can still increase flood peaks at catchment scale through flood-wave synchrony (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff partially synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); restoration at the wrong reach worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects and in some scenarios raised aggregate flood damages above the baseline (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); and moving the same project downstream along the channel turned a 14% peak reduction into about a 1% increase (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4). Rewetting also consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels for winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost). Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. The state-dependence statements (ev_wgy_ram_10, ev_wgy_ram_11, ev_wgy_ram_12) are guidance-level synthesis, two with their own references and one an expert assertion; they establish that the sign depends on the peat's starting state, on top of its catchment position, but not how often each case occurs. The 30% review average credits the whole river-and-floodplain bundle - river restoration, floodplain and wetland restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage - not wetland restoration alone; it is a peak, not a stage, figure from a corpus that is mostly European and largely British, and its statement that the reduction is larger in larger catchments sits against the catchment-scale nulls above (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Provenance: a temperate, high-income corpus of UK and US catchments almost without exception, with no measured low-income or lower-middle-income result in scope, and a benefit that reaches downstream receptors rather than the plot.

effect_mechanism: The only mechanism this scope's evidence names is hydraulic roughness and storage: wooded wetlands in particular increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time (ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland), alongside an expert statement that wetland protection and restoration buffer communities by reducing wave damage and floods (ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2). Neither unit measures a flood outcome in this scope.
conditionality: The review supplying the mechanism also supplies the base rate: many papers report wetlands reducing floods, some conclude no impact, and others find evidence of wetlands increasing floods (ev_wetflA_acre_heterogeneity). Where a benefit would have to show up it has not — drain blocking has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null) — an on-site storage gain can still raise flood peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment), and during major catastrophic floods the presence or absence of wetlands makes no difference (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The roughness that lowers the peak raises the water: changing floodplain vegetation from wet meadow to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same flood (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up). Provenance: a mixed-income pooling of UK, US, Canadian, Irish and Zimbabwean settings inside a single review plus a global policy brief, with no measurement specific to any of them, and a benefit that falls downstream rather than on the plot.

effect_mechanism: Salt marsh dissipates wave energy and takes height off a surge as it travels across the platform. Wave heights fall by 72% across salt marsh, with a 95% confidence interval of 62 to 79% in a meta-analysis of field measurements (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1); up to 82% of wave energy is dissipated over marsh against 29% over the adjacent sand flat (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_3); storm-surge attenuation rates run from 1.7 to 25 cm per kilometre of marsh depending on marsh and storm characteristics (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_1). The contrast is consistent — salt marsh vegetation had a significant positive effect on wave attenuation, and every paired study comparing vegetated marsh with intertidal mudflat concluded attenuation is greater over the marsh (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_1, ev_flood_hazard_shep11_2). Farmland gives a further view: on the Queensland coast after a cyclone, croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes experienced lower surface water presence compared with more distant areas (ev_flood_hazard_rowl26w1_1).
conditionality: What has been measured is wave attenuation under ordinary conditions: the meta-analysed measurements are all taken under normal conditions of low waves (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1). The function weakens where protection is wanted — attenuation works less effectively during extreme storms lasting more than a day, which the review reads as a reason not to rely on nature-based flood defences alone in populated low-lying coastal and estuarine areas (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_2). Floodwater attenuation inside the marsh, meaning flood-peak reduction and floodwater storage, has never been quantified: the systematic review found no study evaluating it (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_5). Siting can cancel the benefit, since levees and dikes behind a marsh cause water to set up against the structure and limit the surge-attenuating effect (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_4). The remaining support is self-reported: 41% of salt-marsh projects state that such habitats provide improved protection from storm events (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). The Queensland result is an association around existing mangrove and tidal marsh together, read from a satellite surface-water index that does not separate surge from rain flooding; the authors say it does not provide direct evidence of causal protection, and the binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to their models (ev_flood_hazard_rowl26w1_4). Provenance: existing marsh rather than restored marsh, on Australian, US, UK, Dutch, Belgian, Italian and Vietnamese coasts, with coastal property and society as the beneficiary rather than the farm, apart from the Queensland cropland result.

effect_mechanism: Created storage intercepts part of the storm volume before it reaches the receptor: the review reports that reduction of peak discharge by online and offline storage areas is effective and notable in both fieldwork and modelling results (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective), online storage being blocking within the drainage network and offline storage being retention and detention features set aside from the channel.
conditionality: That sentence is the entire evidence base for this cell, and the review qualifies it immediately: the location of offline storage features is the most important factor, depending on soil type and on the number and spatial distribution of the features in the catchment (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective). A creation programme that does not site its features deliberately has no claim on the result. There is no measured outcome for a created wetland here, no second source, and nothing on how the effect behaves as events get rarer. Provenance: UK and European, temperate and high-income, so transfer to a tropical or smallholder catchment is an assumption rather than a finding, and the benefit is downstream rather than on the plot.

effect_mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
conditionality: The measurements are plot to micro-catchment; the catchment-scale benefit is not demonstrated. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), drain blocking has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). Position decides the sign: upland wetlands tend to be flood-generating areas, frequently saturated with little water storage potential (ev_wetflA_acre_position_upland); blanket bogs close to saturation for most of the year rarely attenuate flow and are much more likely to contribute to storm runoff (ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); and an on-site storage gain can still raise peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment). Even on the hillslope the lever is conditional: ditch blocking in upland peat reduces flow peaks only in the steepest, smoothest drains, with the roughness of the surrounding vegetated peat mattering more than the ditches (ev_wetflA_dads_ditchblock_conditional), and upland ditches may increase or decrease local flood peaks depending on layout, topography and synchronisation (ev_wetflA_dads_ditch_sign_flip). The review covering this family reports moderate flood-reduction results but without empirical evidence for larger-scale effects (ev_wetflA_zhu_peatland_confidence). Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. The state-dependence statements (ev_wgy_ram_10, ev_wgy_ram_11, ev_wgy_ram_12) are guidance-level synthesis, two with their own references and one an expert assertion; they establish that the sign depends on the peat's starting state, on top of its catchment position, but not how often each case occurs. Provenance: UK blanket peat carries almost the whole cell, with a Chinese high-altitude degradation case and a Newfoundland bog; temperate and high-income, with no low-income or lower-middle-income measurement, and a benefit that arrives downstream rather than on the plot.

justification.mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
justification.conditionality: The measurements are plot to micro-catchment; the catchment-scale benefit is not demonstrated. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), drain blocking has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). Position decides the sign: upland wetlands tend to be flood-generating areas, frequently saturated with little water storage potential (ev_wetflA_acre_position_upland); blanket bogs close to saturation for most of the year rarely attenuate flow and are much more likely to contribute to storm runoff (ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); and an on-site storage gain can still raise peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment). Even on the hillslope the lever is conditional: ditch blocking in upland peat reduces flow peaks only in the steepest, smoothest drains, with the roughness of the surrounding vegetated peat mattering more than the ditches (ev_wetflA_dads_ditchblock_conditional), and upland ditches may increase or decrease local flood peaks depending on layout, topography and synchronisation (ev_wetflA_dads_ditch_sign_flip). The review covering this family reports moderate flood-reduction results but without empirical evidence for larger-scale effects (ev_wetflA_zhu_peatland_confidence). Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. The state-dependence statements (ev_wgy_ram_10, ev_wgy_ram_11, ev_wgy_ram_12) are guidance-level synthesis, two with their own references and one an expert assertion; they establish that the sign depends on the peat's starting state, on top of its catchment position, but not how often each case occurs. Provenance: UK blanket peat carries almost the whole cell, with a Chinese high-altitude degradation case and a Newfoundland bog; temperate and high-income, with no low-income or lower-middle-income measurement, and a benefit that arrives downstream rather than on the plot.

effect_mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplain and depressional wetland puts storm water somewhere other than the channel. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% at the reach scale, and by up to 19% where banks were lowered furthest (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_6); wooded wetlands increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time (ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland); depressional wetlands could store 72% of the total runoff volume of a 2-year rainfall event (ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage); and in the loss frame, embanking a floodplain to remove its storage raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). A systematic review adds an average flood peak reduction of 30% for river and floodplain management, a bundle of measures of which floodplain and wetland restoration is a part (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Peak and stage are separate outcomes that move apart: removing the levees lowered cross-sectional water-surface elevation by an average of 0.66 m (ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1) while decreasing peak discharge over the same segment by less than 0.04 to 0.13% (ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_3), and roughening the floodplain with shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same flood (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up).
conditionality: The clear evidence is explicitly local and explicitly for moderate rainfall events (ev_wetflA_dads_summary_moderate); for the most extreme events, and at large catchment scales, the evidence does not suggest a major effect on downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null, ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null), during major catastrophic floods the presence or absence of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null), and the storable share of a flood falls with rarity — the same depressional wetlands held 72% of the runoff volume of a 2-year event but 41% of a 100-year event (ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage). At the catchment outlet the modelled changes are small: 0.65% off the Q100 peak, 1.1% off the Q25 peak, and no change in flood volume for the Q2 storm (ev_flood_hazard_worl23_2, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_3, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_4), with only modest attenuation of peak flows across the design storms because of the steep, flashy setting (ev_flood_hazard_worl23_1); and the aggregated effects of multiple wetlands can differ considerably from the functions observed at individual wetland scale (ev_wetflA_thor_scale_mismatch). The sign flips with position: upstream wetland obviously amplified downstream flood risks while downstream wetland was the part the authors would restore first (ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4); restoring many reaches had no effect on property damages and some worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_3, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); headwater wetlands fill during relatively normal summer rain, which spends the capacity they would need for a much larger event, whereas downstream wetlands that stay dry keep that buffering capacity (ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_2, ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_1). Rewetting itself consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — a wet wetland and an empty flood store are competing objectives. The 30% review average credits the whole river-and-floodplain bundle - river restoration, floodplain and wetland restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage - not wetland restoration alone; it is a peak, not a stage, figure from a corpus that is mostly European and largely British, and its statement that the reduction is larger in larger catchments sits against the catchment-scale nulls above (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Provenance: temperate and high-income, UK, US and Swedish, with a Chinese basin model; the sole lower-middle-income measurement in scope is a reversal, Zimbabwean headwater dambos protected because they are assumed to reduce floods but measured as the principal mechanism of storm-discharge generation (ev_wetflA_acre_dambo_reversal). The benefit is off-plot in every case.

effect_mechanism: Restoration widens the gap where the restored land was itself farmed or where wildlife from the restored wetland reaches neighbouring fields. Rewetted peat becomes unsuitable for crops such as potatoes and carrots [ev_wgy_qa_6], drainage-based agriculture cannot be combined with high water tables in the same peatland [ev_wgy_ram_17], and paludicrops are mostly non-edible, so the transition can mean a local net loss of food production [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]. Near the protected Poyang Lake wetland, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by migratory birds and other wild animals with no compensation [ev_wgy_poy_2]. Against this, in Uganda the matched GCF evaluation found the aggregate yield effect positive but not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5], and in Ghana clearing a 7 km creek to the Songor lagoon enhanced cattle farming along it [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2].
conditionality: The loss is local, not national: a Finnish study found only minor impact on national food production but local challenges in peatland-rich municipalities [ev_wgy_qa_5]. Most of the negative evidence is expert assertion from European peatland policy briefs; the only matched counterfactual in a low-income country shows no yield change either way. Expect a production cost where restoration converts farmed land (drained peat, reclaimed lakebed); expect little change where it restores already-degraded, uncultivated wetland.

The Uganda GCF evaluation, a matched comparison, found that a broader crop portfolio around restored wetlands gave a positive but not statistically significant change in aggregate yield [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5]. conditionality: Neither unit may set a class. Both describe existing mangrove and tidal marsh, which the authors could not separate, not a restored or managed wetland, and the outcome is crop cover read from a satellite vegetation index, not yield or production. The binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to the models [ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_3], and the authors say the results do not provide direct evidence of causal protection. It is a single high-income Australian study in which only two crop types, irrigated sugarcane and mango, were present, so nothing here speaks to rainfed smallholder production gaps.

The binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to the models [ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_3], and the authors say the results do not provide direct evidence of causal protection. It is a single high-income Australian study in which only two crop types, irrigated sugarcane and mango, were present, so nothing here speaks to rainfed smallholder production gaps.

effect_mechanism: There are two horizons. In the short term, rewetting ends drainage-based cropping: food crops such as potatoes and carrots become unsuitable [ev_wgy_qa_6], high and low water-table uses cannot share a peatland [ev_wgy_ram_17], and paludicrops are mostly non-edible [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]; Finland reports a minor national but a local effect [ev_wgy_qa_5]. In the long term, keeping peat drained also loses production: subsidence on deep SE Asian peat may cause loss of agricultural production once gravity drainage fails [ev_agricultural_production_value_hooi12_3], and the drained Mega Rice Project land proved largely unsuitable for rice, threatening local livelihoods [ev_agricultural_production_value_ritz13_9].
conditionality: The class and its evidence disagree in kind. The positive direction comes from studies of draining tropical peat (oil palm, Acacia, the Mega Rice Project), which document the cost of keeping peat drained, not a measured yield after rewetting; it is an avoided-future-loss argument. The measured-style evidence on rewetting itself, all European, points to a near-term production loss. No low-income source. Treat as: rewetting costs production now and may avoid larger losses later on deep, subsiding tropical peat.

effect_mechanism: Floodplain and lakebed restoration costs production mainly by bringing wildlife onto nearby farmland: at Poyang Lake, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by migratory birds and other wild animals and they cannot be compensated [ev_wgy_poy_2]. Elsewhere the effect is neutral to positive: Uganda's matched evaluation found a positive but not significant yield change [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5], and reconnecting a creek in Ghana enhanced cattle farming [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. Restored wetlands themselves recover slowly: nitrogen storage remained significantly lower than in reference wetlands for 30 y [ev_soil_nitrogen_mm12_4].
conditionality: The negative weight comes from a single upper-middle-income survey (Poyang) where compensation goes to landowners rather than to the tenants who bear the crop damage, which is a design problem that targeting could fix. The low-income evidence shows no measurable yield loss. The soil-nitrogen shortfall is an ecological recovery finding, not a farm yield.

effect_mechanism: Two kinds of recurring cost sit in this pool. The first is a land payment in a US national model: where wetlands are restored on farmland, land rental costs cover the opportunity cost of land removed from agricultural production, and for cropland they are, in the mean, more than five times greater than those for pastureland, at US$274 ± 156 per hectare [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6]. Design, construction and maintenance enter the same framework as area-dependent costs annualised over a 50-year management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%, with the rental rates taken from state-level agricultural statistics across the 48 contiguous states. The second is upkeep: evidence compiled in the cost-effectiveness review suggests that annual monitoring costs are typically around 20% of the initial restoration investment for floodplain restoration in the USA, and mangrove restoration in the Philippines and Vietnam [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_11].
conditionality: This is a modelled national cost framework for constructed nutrient-retention wetlands, and the recurring item prices forgone agriculture on US cropland, a high-income economy; it cannot be read across to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, where the opportunity cost of farmland is set by quite different land and tenure arrangements. No currency year is stated in the quoted passage. The monitoring share is a cited summary, not a measurement from these projects, and it is expressed relative to the initial investment, so it scales with however large that establishment cost was. The useful point is structural: where wetlands are restored on farmland, the standing cost is the production forgone, not the upkeep of the works. The Taillardat per-hectare-per-year medians formerly pooled here are total project capital annualised over the restoration event and now sit in establishment cost (the cost-routing rule) [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6].

effect_mechanism: Household income has been found both to rise and to fall with wetland restoration, through different channels. Losses follow land taken out of farming: at Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake saw per capita income fall by 0.338 log points in the matched comparison, and the authors report a significant negative impact on household income [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_6]; in a separate Poyang survey 56.9% of households said income decreased after joining the compensation policy, 38.3% no change and only 4.8% an increase, attributed to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]. Newer accounts add to the loss side: in Germany, rewetting grassland with no further cultivation left losses in farm gross margin varying from 1 to 181 percent and an average of 35 percent per farm [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1]. In Uganda, the Green Climate Fund evaluation found that early changes did not translate into measurable improvements in income, and total income was lower among treated households at the 10 per cent level [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2]. On drained peat, paludiculture is generally not profitable at farm level on biomass sales alone, it is hard to keep income at the conventional level, and SE Asian oil palm communities face lower returns under rewetting [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1, ev_wet_econret_temm26_4, ev_household_income_mish21_5]. Gains come from payments, wages and products that sell: Poyang households gained transfer income (ATT 0.717) [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4]; Working for Wetlands in South Africa employed people previously without stable income, and at Manalana a cost-benefit analysis compared provisioning benefits to local households with rehabilitation cost [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_economic_return_bbr_2]; high-value niche products (Sphagnum founder material, thatching reed) can be profitable [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2, ev_wgy_wich_6]; in Uzbekistan, revived fish, muskrat skin and reed production gave residents a substantial increase in income [ev_household_income_uzicr_1]; and in Belarus indirect benefits reached agro-ecotourism businesses and wild-berry marketing [ev_wgy_blr_2]. Newer project accounts add to the gain side: converting arable land to grassland and rewetting it changed German farm gross margin from -90 to +84 percent, an average increase of 5 percent [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_2]; in Viet Nam's U Minh Thuong buffer zone, Green Contracts for alternative fire-free income sources resulted in a doubling of annual incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1]; in Riau, 75% of the 152 respondents registered monthly income increase of more than USD 35 from selling community-garden harvest [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2]; and in South Sumatra fishponds inside a rewetted canal system generated 18,700,000 IDR from the 2019 harvest, which the authors call not yet optimal [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1].
conditionality: What separates the sides, in the evidence's own terms, is how the restoration is paid for and who bears the cost. The losses are where farmland is retired and compensation is small or absent [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; the gains are wages on restoration works, compensation transfers, alternative livelihoods and niche products [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. Time also matters: the Poyang loss was no longer significant by the later panel round [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. For a Task Team Leader the design levers are compensation sized to the forgone farm income, paid to the people who actually farm the land, and a product or wage channel built in. Three things weaken the positive side as household evidence. The Poyang transfer gain is one component of the same households' income, whose total fell, so it is not an independent finding [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4]. Several gains are society-level, not household, and are held out of the class for that reason: the floodplain-restoration benefit-cost ratio of at least 5-to-1 counts reduced flood damages [ev_economic_return_gour20_2]; about 40% of salt marsh projects recover their cost within 30 years, sooner once carbon value is added [ev_economic_return_wang22_5, ev_economic_return_wang22_6]; salt-marsh nature-based defences are compared on cost with breakwaters, and are limited to low wave heights and not always cost effective [ev_economic_return_nara16_3, ev_economic_return_nara16_6, ev_economic_return_nara16_5]; and the benefits of fully rewetting drained agricultural peatlands were estimated to outweigh restoration costs at society level [ev_wgy_qa_7]. Income households already draw from existing wetlands is not counted here either, as it is not a gain from restoration. The matched household studies sit on the negative side; on the null side, in Kabale, Uganda, the national wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1], and in Belarus no direct household benefit was found because none was designed [ev_wgy_blr_1]. The newer units sharpen the separator. A Central Kalimantan report of income losses in villages that had stopped fire use was rejected at review by Pete Steward, who was not confident it could be included, and is no longer counted; the row stays split without it. The German figures are modelled typical farms in a high-income economy, and the arable-to-grassland gain is driven by conversion payments, not by the rewetted land producing anything [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1, ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_2]. The Vietnamese and Riau gains come from alternative livelihoods - fruit, vegetables, fish, livestock, community gardens - bundled with the restoration rather than from the restored peat, are self-reported, and have no comparison group [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1, ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2]; the Sumatran fish income is a total for a community demonstration project, not a household figure [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1]. The Indonesian social cost-benefit results are held out of the class because they are societal welfare with carbon priced in, not household income: enhanced rewetting with paludiculture yielded a lower average NPV over 25 years but a higher average NPV over 50 years [ev_wet_econret_jali25_1], and restoration through paludiculture offered superior ecosystem services compared with oil-palm monoculture [ev_wet_econret_jali25_3].

effect_mechanism: The matched evidence in low-income settings shows no household gain. The Uganda GCF evaluation found that awareness, crop diversification and adaptation changes did not translate into measurable improvements in income, assets or food security; total income was lower among treated households, significant at the 10 per cent level, while crop-farming income was close to zero difference and food-security indicators showed no significant difference [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3, ev_food_security_fp034e_4]. conditionality: The sides are a matched evaluation and a completion-report assertion, and they differ in what the wetland gave households. effect_mechanism: On rewetted peat, household income has been found to hold up or rise where a product sells or a payment is made, and to fall where neither is in place. High-value products such as Sphagnum founder material, thatching reed and directly marketed water buffalo products can be profitable [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2, ev_wgy_wich_5, ev_wgy_wich_6], tropical paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit [ev_economic_return_tan21_10], and an SDG mapping asserts that land-users maintain income through biomass and nature-based payments, if available [ev_wet_hhinc_temm26_6]. Payments and alternative livelihoods carry the other recorded gains: converting German arable land to grassland and rewetting it changed gross margin from -90 to +84 percent, an average increase of 5 percent [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_2]; in Viet Nam's U Minh Thuong buffer zone, Green Contracts for alternative fire-free income sources resulted in a doubling of annual incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1]; in Riau, 75% of the 152 respondents registered monthly income increase of more than USD 35 from selling community-garden harvest [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2]; and in South Sumatra fishponds inside a rewetted canal system generated 18,700,000 IDR from the 2019 harvest, not yet optimal by the authors' account [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1]. Losses are recorded for some adopters and are reported here as harm, not averaged away: paludiculture is generally not profitable at farm level when revenue relies solely on biomass sales [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1], income is hard to keep at the conventional level [ev_wet_econret_temm26_4], seasonal water-table raising restricts management in ways that reduce farm income [ev_household_income_cxc_5], SE Asian oil palm communities face lower returns under rewetting [ev_household_income_mish21_5], in Germany, rewetting grassland with no further cultivation left losses in farm gross margin varying from 1 to 181 percent and an average of 35 percent per farm [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1], and farmed Sphagnum cannot compete with peat as growing media [ev_wgy_wich_4]. Harvesting existing reed stands shows the spread within a crop: thatching bundles have a mode of € 572 ha-1 a-1 with a risk of loss below 1 %, combustion bales a mode of € 53 with an 18 % risk of loss, and biogas chaff a loss in the mode (€ 195 ha-1 a-1) with a 98 % risk of loss because demand and price are low [ev_wgy_wich_1, ev_wgy_wich_2, ev_wgy_wich_3].

effect_mechanism: Marsh vegetation attenuates waves and currents as water passes through the canopy, so suspended sediment settles, the bed accretes and surface elevation is maintained while lateral erosion of the shoreline is reduced. That mechanism is measured from both ends: inside existing marsh against adjacent unvegetated mudflat, where most paired studies reported increased accretion or surface elevation or reduced erosion and the pooled effect on shoreline stabilisation was positive (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4); and in planted marsh, which improved shoreline protection against degraded wetland (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). A field experiment on a wave-stressed shoreline tests the mechanism from the loss side: lateral erosion where aboveground and belowground vegetation was removed (114.19 cm) was significantly higher than in vegetated controls (76.76 cm), whereas removing only the aboveground vegetation made no difference (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_2); across 15 previous comparisons of marsh-edge erosion between vegetated and vegetation-reduced conditions, the mean effect size of 1.22 shows a generally positive effect of vegetation on the reduction of marsh-edge erosion (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_4).
conditionality: Much of the pool is not a restoration result at all: the paired-study evidence measures what EXISTING marsh does against bare mudflat (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4), which is an argument for protecting marsh that is already there rather than a measured gain from creating or replanting it, and a sizeable minority of those paired studies did not report a positive effect. The vegetation-removal experiment and its meta-analysis are the same kind of evidence - what existing marsh loses when its plants go, not what restoration adds - and vegetation had no effect on vertical erosion of the marsh surface (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_3); their outcome is erosion of the marsh edge itself. The restored-versus-degraded pooled values are effect sizes and shares of studies whose scale the sources do not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3), which is why direction is firmer than magnitude here. This is shoreline and tidal-flat erosion only - it carries nothing about soil loss from cropland or rangeland - and the field sites are high-income coasts in the United States, United Kingdom, China and the Netherlands, with the authors noting that matched restored and degraded pairs are few.

effect_mechanism: Re-vegetating bare blanket peat, alone or together with gully blocking by stone and timber dams, is the peatland practice behind this row. On the only quantity measured here - the share of storm rainfall leaving as storm discharge - restoration changed nothing at either restored site relative to the bare, unrestored control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null).
conditionality: The no-relationship class rests on that null alone, and it is about water volume, not soil. The unit behind this row is a runoff-coefficient null (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), and the paper's own conclusion is that restoration altered the timing and peak of storm delivery while leaving the volume of runoff produced unchanged. It is therefore evidence that re-vegetation and gully blocking did not reduce how much water ran off, and it should not be read as evidence that they fail to reduce erosion - no sediment or soil-loss measurement is present in this pool, which is why the cell states no relationship rather than a reduction, and the row stands as an evidence gap. The observation comes from an upland English blanket-peat site in a high-income temperate setting, with no tropical peat and no farmland, so this row marks an evidence gap rather than a finding of no effect.
