effect_mechanism: The service is physical and biological at once: water is made to pass slowly through a created or restored wetland, sediment settles, plants take up nutrients and denitrification removes nitrogen. Across the created and restored wetlands reviewed, median removal rates were 93 g of total nitrogen and 1.2 g of total phosphorus per square metre per year [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_1, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_2], median removal efficiency was 37% of the incoming nitrogen load (95% confidence interval 29-44%) and 46% of the phosphorus load (37-55%) [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4], and the review's own summary is that created wetlands generally remove both and that overall removal efficiency is roughly 40% [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_5]. Measured on created riverine basins, nitrate removal was 42% in the tenth year and soluble reactive phosphorus retention stayed around 70% [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. A meta-analysis of phosphorus retention gives a median of 31.4% of total phosphorus and 28.6% of phosphate retained by restored/constructed wetlands across all hydrologic regimes [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_3, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_4]. Against the realistic counterfactual the same holds: restoration raised the water-quality regulating service by 31% over degraded wetlands [ev_nutrient_removal_meli14_5], and nutrient and carbon loads were lower from restored peat extraction sites than from abandoned ones [ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5]. Where the wetlands are put multiplies all of this: a spatially targeted increase in United States wetland area by 10 per cent would double wetland nitrogen removal [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2] and give an estimated 54 per cent decrease in nitrogen loading in nitrate-affected watersheds [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3], and placing wetlands where the nitrogen surplus is highest provides approximately 40 times more removal than placing them on non-agricultural land, at nearly double the cost [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4], with removal rising linearly up to roughly a 15% increase in wetland area before targeting runs out of high-surplus land [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5]. Floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration scenarios met a watershed's required phosphorus load reduction on predicted storage [ev_nutrient_removal_worl23_5], and designing for nitrogen retention did not cost species richness [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6]. Project and synthesis sources add the same direction in other settings. On Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual retention is about 17 tons of nitrogen and 3.0 tons of phosphorus, from inlet and outlet concentrations and an assumed mean annual flow-through [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]; on Bulgaria's restored Belene Island marshes a first, preliminary test indicated a reduction in nutrients in outflow water [ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3]; and the Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, states that disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow [ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7].
conditionality: The setting a rural scan would target is the setting where the phosphorus side of this can reverse. Total phosphorus removal was significantly different from zero for every wetland-history group except wetlands restored on formerly drained cropland, for which there was an insignificant net release of phosphorus [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7]; negative phosphorus removal rates were reported in 17 of 146 wetlands, six of them created on former cropland and one on previous cattle pasture, whose soil is usually rich in phosphorus that may be released after construction [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6]. An annual release rather than removal of nitrogen appears in a very small number of studies, while negative phosphorus rates are less uncommon [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9], and in 17 individual cases the confidence limits encompassed the zero-effect line, including one whose average indicated a release of nitrogen [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8]. The phosphorus meta-analysis carries both sides in a single pool. The median wetland retains phosphorus, yet out of 273 wetland site-years 16% have negative total phosphorus retention and 25% negative phosphate retention - the wetland exported more than it received [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_2]; phosphorus releases are most common in restored/constructed wetlands and wetlands with unregulated, precipitation-driven inflow [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_7]; and despite the predominance of wetlands as net phosphorus sinks on an annual basis, 75% of wetlands with monthly data are a total phosphorus source for at least one month and 39% for three consecutive months or more [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_8]. What separates retention from release, in this source's terms, is the wetland type and the inflow regime: a restored wetland fed by unregulated, rain-driven inflow is where release is most common. That pool merges restored with constructed wetlands, is mostly young wetlands, and is biased toward North America and Europe. Rewetting peat carries its own reversals, both from the Ramsar report's cited synthesis: in some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term [ev_wgy_ram_8]; and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, called internal eutrophication [ev_wgy_ram_9]. A rural scan aimed at farmed peat should expect both. Age is the second condition: in the tenth year after construction total phosphorus decreased by only 2% in one basin and increased by 14% in the other, after a consistent pattern of retention during the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4], and sediment and total phosphorus retention showed signs of diminishing after 10 years of river flow even while nitrate and soluble reactive phosphorus retention held [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5]. Not every restoration touches water quality at all: blocking gullies on an eroding upland peatland had no significant positive impact on water quality and left a non-significant increase in dissolved organic carbon [ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null]. Finally, the largest numbers in the row are modelled national scenarios rather than measurements [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4], the efficiencies vary with hydraulic loading and temperature, the inflows behind them include treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3], the Moldovan retention is an estimate built on an assumed flow-through, the Bulgarian result is a single preliminary test with further monitoring said to be needed [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1, ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3], and every quantified unit comes from Europe or North America.

Measured on created riverine basins, nitrate removal was 42% in the tenth year and soluble reactive phosphorus retention stayed around 70% [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. A meta-analysis of phosphorus retention gives a median of 31.4% of total phosphorus and 28.6% of phosphate retained by restored/constructed wetlands across all hydrologic regimes [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_3, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_4]. Against the realistic counterfactual the same holds: restoration raised the water-quality regulating service by 31% over degraded wetlands [ev_nutrient_removal_meli14_5], and nutrient and carbon loads were lower from restored peat extraction sites than from abandoned ones [ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5]. Where the wetlands are put multiplies all of this: a spatially targeted increase in United States wetland area by 10 per cent would double wetland nitrogen removal [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2] and give an estimated 54 per cent decrease in nitrogen loading in nitrate-affected watersheds [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3], and placing wetlands where the nitrogen surplus is highest provides approximately 40 times more removal than placing them on non-agricultural land, at nearly double the cost [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4], with removal rising linearly up to roughly a 15% increase in wetland area before targeting runs out of high-surplus land [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5]. Floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration scenarios met a watershed's required phosphorus load reduction on predicted storage [ev_nutrient_removal_worl23_5], and designing for nitrogen retention did not cost species richness [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6]. Project and synthesis sources add the same direction in other settings. On Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual retention is about 17 tons of nitrogen and 3.0 tons of phosphorus, from inlet and outlet concentrations and an assumed mean annual flow-through [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]; on Bulgaria's restored Belene Island marshes a first, preliminary test indicated a reduction in nutrients in outflow water [ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3]; and the Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, states that disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow [ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7].
justification.conditionality: The setting a rural scan would target is the setting where the phosphorus side of this can reverse. Total phosphorus removal was significantly different from zero for every wetland-history group except wetlands restored on formerly drained cropland, for which there was an insignificant net release of phosphorus [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7]; negative phosphorus removal rates were reported in 17 of 146 wetlands, six of them created on former cropland and one on previous cattle pasture, whose soil is usually rich in phosphorus that may be released after construction [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6]. An annual release rather than removal of nitrogen appears in a very small number of studies, while negative phosphorus rates are less uncommon [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9], and in 17 individual cases the confidence limits encompassed the zero-effect line, including one whose average indicated a release of nitrogen [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8]. The phosphorus meta-analysis carries both sides in a single pool. The median wetland retains phosphorus, yet out of 273 wetland site-years 16% have negative total phosphorus retention and 25% negative phosphate retention - the wetland exported more than it received [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_2]; phosphorus releases are most common in restored/constructed wetlands and wetlands with unregulated, precipitation-driven inflow [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_7]; and despite the predominance of wetlands as net phosphorus sinks on an annual basis, 75% of wetlands with monthly data are a total phosphorus source for at least one month and 39% for three consecutive months or more [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_8]. What separates retention from release, in this source's terms, is the wetland type and the inflow regime: a restored wetland fed by unregulated, rain-driven inflow is where release is most common. That pool merges restored with constructed wetlands, is mostly young wetlands, and is biased toward North America and Europe. Rewetting peat carries its own reversals, both from the Ramsar report's cited synthesis: in some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term [ev_wgy_ram_8]; and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, called internal eutrophication [ev_wgy_ram_9]. A rural scan aimed at farmed peat should expect both. Age is the second condition: in the tenth year after construction total phosphorus decreased by only 2% in one basin and increased by 14% in the other, after a consistent pattern of retention during the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4], and sediment and total phosphorus retention showed signs of diminishing after 10 years of river flow even while nitrate and soluble reactive phosphorus retention held [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5]. Not every restoration touches water quality at all: blocking gullies on an eroding upland peatland had no significant positive impact on water quality and left a non-significant increase in dissolved organic carbon [ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null]. Finally, the largest numbers in the row are modelled national scenarios rather than measurements [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4], the efficiencies vary with hydraulic loading and temperature, the inflows behind them include treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3], the Moldovan retention is an estimate built on an assumed flow-through, the Bulgarian result is a single preliminary test with further monitoring said to be needed [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1, ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3], and every quantified unit comes from Europe or North America.

effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping catchments a wetland works as an interception point for the nutrients leaving the fields. In the 10th year after construction, average nitrate removal by the created riverine basins was 42%, the highest of the decade [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1], and soluble reactive phosphorus retention continued to be significant at around 70%, 63% in the planted basin and 73% in the naturally colonising one, with no significant difference between them [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. In Swedish farmland, nutrient retention and diversity proved compatible aims, since biodiversity was neither locally nor regionally harmed by high nitrate levels [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6].
conditionality: Phosphorus is where this fails. By the 10th year total phosphorus showed little retention and even export, falling by only 2% in the naturally colonising basin and rising by 14% in the planted one, after a consistent pattern of retention over the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4]: the created wetland had become a net phosphorus exporter in its tenth year. Sediment and total phosphorus retention were diminishing after 10 years of river flow [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5], so the particulate fraction of the service decays as the basin fills while the dissolved-nutrient service persists. Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Ohio and Sweden, and both concern created wetlands fed by river or catchment water rather than restored ones; the Ohio basins were continuously pumped, which is not how a wetland in a farmed catchment is fed. Nothing was measured in a tropical or lower-income rainfed system.

effect_mechanism: A planted salt-marsh canopy slows tidal flow and waves, so suspended particles and the nutrients and contaminants bound to them drop out of the water column and are trapped in the marsh instead of moving on. The measured expression of that here is sediment trapping by planted marsh, which matched or bettered the adjacent natural marsh (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15).
conditionality: The row rests on a single meta-analytic estimate that its own authors hedge, and the comparison is against adjacent NATURAL marsh - so it says a planted marsh traps sediment at least as well as an intact one, not what the gain is over an unvegetated shore or over doing nothing. Sediment trapping is also a proxy for particulate and turbidity load, not a measurement of nutrient or contaminant removal; nothing in this pool measures nitrogen or phosphorus. The underlying studies are concentrated in North America, Europe and East Asia and are high-income coastal settings, with no observation from a low- or lower-middle-income farmed catchment, and the practice is marsh planting dominated by a single genus - a different intervention from the inland nutrient-retention wetlands that carry the main water-quality case.

effect_mechanism: A created wetland works as a reactor placed in the flow path: residence time rises, nitrogen is removed by plant uptake and denitrification and phosphorus settles with sediment, so a share of the incoming load leaves the water. Across created and restored freshwater wetlands that is a measured net removal of total nitrogen and total phosphorus, both as mass rates and as a share of the incoming load (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_1, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_2, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_5), and nitrate and soluble-reactive-phosphorus retention persisted into the tenth year of a created riverine pair (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3). Where new wetlands are put matters more than how many: modelled placement in the highest nitrogen-surplus areas removes far more nitrogen than placement on non-agricultural land, at a higher cost because it takes cropland out of production (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3), and the gain flattens as restoration spreads beyond the hotspots (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5). Created wetlands can be designed to hold nutrients and carry species diversity at the same time rather than trading them off (ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6).
conditionality: Creating a wetland on nutrient-enriched farmland can reverse the sign. Negative phosphorus removal - the wetland exporting phosphorus rather than retaining it - was reported in a minority of the reviewed wetlands, and most of those had been created on former cropland or cattle pasture, where soil rich in phosphorus from its cropping history can release after construction (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6); the rest were new wetlands released from initially phosphorus-rich sediments. That is the setting a rural scan targets, so legacy soil phosphorus belongs in the design brief. At site level a created basin exported total phosphorus in its tenth year while its twin barely retained any, after years of consistent retention (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3), and sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment and phosphorus services age out while the nitrogen service holds. A substantial minority of individual wetlands showed no demonstrable nitrogen removal (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8), and net annual release of nitrogen, though rare, has been observed (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9). The quantified ceiling claims are modelled, not measured, and every unit is high-income temperate - inflows in the review included treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff, so the pooled efficiency is not a farmland-only number.

effect_mechanism: Rewetting a cut-over peat site - raising the water table, filling or blocking ditches, mulching and transferring a moss layer - stabilises the water table and keeps the exposed peat saturated, so less nutrient and carbon load is flushed from the surface. Against the realistic do-nothing counterfactual of an abandoned extraction site, the loads leaving restored sites were lower (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). The Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, generalises this: disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow (ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7).
conditionality: The gain is measured against the degraded starting point, and against that baseline restored extraction sites leak less (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). Measured against their intact natural counterparts the same restored sites leaked more nutrients and carbon, associated with greater water-table variation (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_4); that is incomplete recovery towards an intact peatland, not harm, and the two comparisons must not be netted. The real reversals are in the Ramsar report's cited synthesis. In some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term (ev_wgy_ram_8); and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens, rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, internal eutrophication (ev_wgy_ram_9). Agricultural peat is exactly the land a rural scan would target, so a downstream nutrient pulse in the early years, and a sustained phosphorus problem on fertilised fens, should be planned for rather than assumed away. The measured case in this pool found no significant water-quality improvement and no significant reduction in aqueous carbon losses after rewetting an eroding upland blanket peat, with dissolved organic carbon rising non-significantly afterwards (ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null); the quantity measured there is dissolved organic carbon routed to the nearest water-quality outcome, not nutrients, and water colour did change. Everything here is boreal or temperate peat in high-income countries or unspecified settings; nothing covers tropical peat or a farmed low- or lower-middle-income catchment, and the Ramsar statements give direction without magnitude or site.

justification.mechanism: Reinstating wetland hydrology puts the nutrient load back in contact with saturated soil and vegetation, where nitrogen is denitrified or taken up and phosphorus is stored with sediment on the floodplain. Modelled floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration met the watershed's regulatory phosphorus reduction requirement on predicted phosphorus storage in every scenario (ev_nutrient_removal_worl23_5); a meta-analysis of phosphorus retention gives a median of 31.4% of total phosphorus and 28.6% of phosphate retained by restored/constructed wetlands across all hydrologic regimes (ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_3, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_4); restoring degraded wetlands raised the water-quality regulating service - retention, removal and breakdown of nutrients - against the degraded state (ev_nutrient_removal_meli14_5); on Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual retention is about 17 tons of nitrogen and 3.0 tons of phosphorus (ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1); on Bulgaria's restored Belene Island marshes a first, preliminary test indicated reduced nutrients in outflow water (ev_nutrient_removal_bgicr_3); and the wetlands already standing across a continent remove a large nitrogen mass each year, with the limit on that removal being a spatial disconnect between where wetlands sit and where the nitrogen is (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_1). The last is a siting argument from existing wetlands rather than a restoration effect, and it points the same way: target the hotspots.
justification.conditionality: The sharpest limit is the land type this tool exists to point at. Grouped by land-use history, wetlands restored on formerly drained cropland were the only group whose phosphorus removal was not significantly different from zero, showing instead an insignificant net release of phosphorus (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7). The phosphorus meta-analysis carries both sides in a single pool. The median wetland retains phosphorus, yet out of 273 wetland site-years 16% have negative total phosphorus retention and 25% negative phosphate retention - the wetland exported more than it received (ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_2); phosphorus releases are most common in restored/constructed wetlands and wetlands with unregulated, precipitation-driven inflow (ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_7); and despite the predominance of wetlands as net phosphorus sinks on an annual basis, 75% of wetlands with monthly data are a total phosphorus source for at least one month and 39% for three consecutive months or more (ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_8). effect_mechanism: A wetland stores water from precipitation and releases it slowly to its surroundings, which can recharge groundwater aquifers [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. On the ground, mean water tables rose significantly at all distance classes after an Exmoor peatland was restored, from just below the surface to above it in the peat pans [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable], and the water-table level of drained peat extraction sites was reported to be successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6]. Project evaluations add managed-water cases. In Belarus, active water regulation held May-June water levels in the Zvanets fen mire during 2021-2022 close to the optimal 5-20 cm above ground despite climate-induced changes in the Polesie region [ev_wgy_blr_5]. In Lao PDR the evidence is engineered rather than restorative: a weir at the Nongdern wetland raised the farmland able to use wetland water from 37.16 ha to 73.47 ha, almost 100 percent [ev_wgy_lao_1], and the evaluators conclude that renovating damaged dykes re-established previously dry lakes and water bodies, raising their water level and surface area for the dry season and other livelihood activities [ev_wgy_lao_2].
conditionality: The near-ditch groundwater evidence, with its small footprint and inconclusive effects outside the wetland soil, now sits in the catchment water yield rows. No unit here measures groundwater under neighbouring farmland, so this row should be read as a change inside and immediately around the wetland. Nor does the hydrology come back whole. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were found difficult to maintain in restored extraction areas, so the level can be restored while its dynamics are not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]; many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the initial few years after restoration because of earlier changes in peat structure and consolidation caused by degradation [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]; at Exmoor the median water-table condition remained similar at all distances, so the significant rise is in the mean and driven by the wettest states rather than by a shift in the typical state [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]; and restoration results vary enough that fieldwork found no significant increase in floodplain water storage or overland flow where modelling showed a 6-fold increase in overland-flow storage volume [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The water-table sources are concentrated in Canada, Finland, Estonia, Ireland, Germany and Great Britain, and the practice behind them is peatland ditch blocking in boreal and temperate landscapes — the relevance of these numbers to a dryland farming system is untested. The only unit that measures water reaching farmland is the Lao weir, which is water-control infrastructure in a Ramsar wetland: its gain is in area served, measured before and after the weir, and says nothing about groundwater beyond the wetland [ev_wgy_lao_1]; the dyke renovation result is the evaluators' conclusion, not a measurement [ev_wgy_lao_2]; and the Belarus water levels are held by active regulation, so they depend on that regulation continuing [ev_wgy_blr_5].

effect_mechanism: In the high-income boreo-temperate evidence, rewetting measurably puts water back where the drain took it from. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at all distance classes, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. conditionality: The recovery is partial. The near-ditch groundwater evidence, with its small footprint and inconclusive effects outside the wetland soil, now sits in the catchment water yield rows. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were difficult to maintain in restored peat-extraction areas, so the level returns but its dynamics do not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]. effect_mechanism: The direction in this scope rests on the general hydrological function rather than on a measured restoration: wetlands store water from precipitation and slowly release it to the surrounding environment, which can recharge groundwater aquifers and maintain atmospheric water cycles [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. Restoring or protecting a wetland is expected to restore that storage and slow release, and so to ease a water deficit downstream of it.
conditionality: This cell is thin, and its units pull in different directions. The positive unit is a functional statement about wetlands in general, offered as a key message rather than as the measured result of any restoration, with no magnitude, no time to effect and no country attached [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. The other is a timescale caveat from a narrative review: numerous studies of peatland rewetting suggest that many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the initial few years after restoration, because of earlier changes in peat structure and consolidation caused by degradation [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. That caveat cuts both ways — short monitoring windows may hide a benefit as easily as they may flatter an early result — but it means nothing here establishes what a restored wetland delivers, to whom, or when. Nothing in this scope measures a farm-level water supply, and neither unit names the income context it was observed in; treat the direction as an expectation to be tested in the pilot rather than as evidence of a delivered gain.
